title: Celtic Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Irish cycles and the Welsh Four Branches mapped as a relationship graph: the Tuatha De Danann and the Fomorians, the Ulster cycle and the Tain, Fionn and the Fianna, and the Mabinogi.

profile.cosmicNature: Layered rather than staged. There is no creation account in the Irish material at all - the world is simply there, and the story starts with people arriving in it. What the tradition has instead is a second world lying alongside this one, reached through a burial mound, a cave, a lake or a sea voyage west, where time runs differently and nobody grows old. It is not above or below. It is the same country, entered sideways.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Deliberately obscured. The Tuatha De Danann are gods in everything but name: they arrive in a cloud, they are masters of every craft, they are immortal until the monks make them otherwise. Christian redactors demoted them to an earlier race of skilled people, or to fallen angels who were not bad enough for hell, and then had them defeated by the ancestors of the Irish and driven into the mounds. So the gods of Ireland reach us as the fairies of Ireland, and the transition is visible in the manuscripts.
profile.afterlife: The Otherworld, and it is not a reward. Tir na nOg, Mag Mell, Emain Ablach - the land of the young, the plain of delight, the isle of apples - are places of feasting where nobody sickens or ages, but they are reached by the living as often as the dead, and going there is dangerous mainly because of time. Oisin comes back after what feels like three years, touches Irish soil, and three centuries land on him at once. Donn's house off the south-west coast gathers the dead, and is the closest thing to a plain underworld.
profile.systemMechanism: Sovereignty, obligation and the word. A king holds the land by marrying its goddess, and if he is unjust or blemished the land itself fails - crops, cattle and milk go with him. Every hero carries geasa, personal prohibitions that are impossible to keep once they multiply, and the tragedies are engineered by forcing a man to break one to honour another. Satire from a poet raises blisters and can end a reign. What is said, promised or forbidden has physical force.
profile.canonTexts: The Mythological Cycle, chiefly Lebor Gabala Erenn and Cath Maige Tuired; the Ulster Cycle, centred on the Tain Bo Cuailnge; the Fenian Cycle around Fionn and the Fianna; the Cycles of the Kings; and, for the Welsh branch, the Four Branches of the Mabinogi with Culhwch and Olwen.

hierarchy.title: The Mother and the Invasions
hierarchy.blurb: There is no creation story. Ireland is simply there, and wave after wave of people arrive, clear the plains, fight the Fomorians and are wiped out - each leaving one survivor to remember it.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The fifth wave arrives in a cloud, and they are gods in everything but name

hierarchy.title: The Tuatha De Danann
hierarchy.blurb: Masters of every craft, demoted by Christian scribes from gods to a magical earlier people. The Dagda is good at things rather than good; Lugh is admitted to Tara only because he is all the trades at once.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: They keep smiths, doctors and war goddesses, and win their wars with better craftsmen

hierarchy.title: The Crafts and the War Furies
hierarchy.blurb: Three gods for metal, wood and bronze, three more for surgery, herbs and the healing well, and three for the fate, the terror and the disorder of a battle. This pantheon divides its labour with unusual precision.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Across the water, a rival aristocracy with a king whose eye kills what it sees

hierarchy.title: The Fomorians
hierarchy.blurb: Not monsters in the earliest material but a people from over the sea, with kings, alliances and marriages into the Tuatha De. Balor's grandson is Lugh, which is why the war is decided by someone who belongs to both sides.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Moytura is won, and then the Milesians come and the gods go under the mounds

hierarchy.title: The Land and the Taking of It
hierarchy.blurb: The island is a woman with three names, and a people takes possession by agreement rather than conquest. Amergin, on the invading side, rules against his own army and makes them win it fairly.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Under the new order, kingship is held by marrying the land - and lost by wronging it

hierarchy.title: The Ulster Cycle
hierarchy.blurb: A king breaks his own guarantee and loses a third of his warriors to exile. They come back guiding an invasion, and every man in Ulster is on the ground with a curse, except one seventeen-year-old.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Later, lighter, and closer to folklore: a warrior band instead of a court

hierarchy.title: The Fenian Cycle
hierarchy.blurb: Fionn burns his thumb on a fish and knows everything. The Fianna hunt, quarrel, elope and are finally broken at Gabhra, and two of them survive to argue about it with Saint Patrick.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Kings judged by the same rule: the land fails when the man on it is unjust

hierarchy.title: Kings, Voyagers and the Welsh Branches
hierarchy.blurb: Conaire breaks every prohibition in one evening by trying to be merciful. Bran sails west and cannot come home. And across the sea, a separate literature: Math, Gwydion, a woman made of flowers, and a head that talks for eighty-seven years.

groups.label: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi

stories.title: The First Battle of Moytura
stories.summary: The Tuatha De arrive in a cloud and burn their ships behind them, and meet the Fir Bolg who already hold Ireland. What follows is conducted with unusual courtesy: envoys are exchanged, the Fir Bolg ask for time to make spears as light as their opponents', and the terms of engagement are agreed. The Tuatha De win, but Nuada loses his hand, and because a king of Ireland must be physically unblemished he can no longer rule. The Fir Bolg survivors are given Connacht rather than destroyed. The victory therefore costs the winners their king immediately, and the crown passes to Bres, which will prove far more expensive than the battle was.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Satire That Deposed a King
stories.summary: Bres is made king because he is beautiful and half-Fomorian, and turns out to be catastrophically mean. He taxes the Tuatha De into servitude, puts the Dagda to digging ditches and Ogma to carrying firewood, and - the charge the text takes most seriously - he does not entertain. The knives of his household are never greased and his people's breath never smells of ale. The poet Cairbre comes and is given a small dark room with no fire, no bed and three dry cakes, and composes the first satire ever made in Ireland. Blisters break out on the king's face, and a blemished king cannot reign. He is deposed by a poem, and goes to the Fomorians for an army.

stories.title: Lugh at the Gate of Tara
stories.summary: A young man arrives at Tara and the doorkeeper asks his art, since no one without one may enter. He offers himself as a wright, and is told they have one; as a smith, a champion, a harper, a warrior, a poet, a historian, a sorcerer, a physician, a cupbearer, a brazier - and each time the answer is the same. Then he asks whether they have any single man who is all of these together, and the door opens. Nuada gives up his seat to him for thirteen days and then permanently, judging him the better man, which is a rare piece of good sense in this literature. Lugh takes command of the coming war and holds a muster in which every craftsman states exactly what he will contribute.

stories.title: The Second Battle of Moytura
stories.summary: The Fomorians come, and the Tuatha De win on logistics as much as valour: Goibniu, Credne and Luchta run a forge beside the field that turns out spears faster than they can be broken, and Dian Cecht's family chant over a well that returns the dead whole. Balor kills Nuada. Then the lid of his eye is levered up, and Lugh puts a sling-stone through it that drives the eye out through the back of his skull so that it destroys the Fomorian ranks behind him. Bres is captured and spared - in exchange for telling the Tuatha De when to plough, sow and reap. The war poem ends as an agricultural text, and then Badb prophesies a world grown old.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Milesians and the Judgement of Amergin
stories.summary: The sons of Mil come to avenge their uncle Ith and meet three goddesses in turn, Banba, Fodla and Eriu, each asking that the island be named for her, and Amergin promises each of them. At Tara the three kings of the Tuatha De ask for judgement, and Amergin - the invaders' own poet - rules against his people: they must withdraw beyond the ninth wave and land again, giving the defenders a fair chance. The Tuatha De raise a storm that drowns several of his brothers, including Donn, who had spoken contemptuously of their magic. Amergin answers the storm with a poem, sets his right foot on the shore, and speaks the verse beginning I am the wind on the sea.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Children of Lir
stories.summary: Lir marries Bodb Derg's daughter Aeb, who bears four children and dies. Her sister Aoife takes her place and grows jealous of how much their father loves them. She takes them to a lake, strikes them with a druid's wand, and turns them into four white swans - leaving them their human voices and their reason, which is the cruelty of it - for nine hundred years: three hundred on Lake Derravaragh, three hundred on the cold Sea of Moyle, three hundred at Erris. Lir can only come to the shore and listen to them singing. Bodb turns Aoife into a demon of the air forever. When the term ends the swans become people again, ancient beyond saving, and are baptised and die.

sources.book: Celtic Myth and Legend, Poetry and Romance

stories.title: The Wooing of Etain
stories.summary: Midir's jealous first wife turns Etain into a pool of water, which becomes a worm, which becomes a purple fly whose humming is sweeter than music. Midir knows the fly is her and carries it with him until a raised wind blows it about Ireland for seven years without rest. It falls at last into the cup of a woman of Ulster, who swallows it and conceives, and Etain is born again as a mortal a thousand and twelve years after her first birth, remembering nothing. She marries the High King Eochaid. Midir comes and plays him at fidchell, losing deliberately and paying handsomely until the last game, then asks his winnings: his arms about Etain, and a kiss. They leave through the roof as swans.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Dream of Aengus
stories.summary: Aengus dreams of a woman standing by his bed and wakes to nothing, and it happens again and again until he sickens for want of her. His parents can do nothing. Bodb Derg searches Ireland for a year and finds her at last on a lake with a hundred and fifty women, all paired and chained in silver: she is Caer Ibormeith, who is a woman one year and a swan the next. Aengus goes to the lake at Samhain when she is in swan form, calls to her, and is told he may have her if he comes to her as she is. He becomes a swan, they circle the lake three times, and fly away together singing music that puts everyone who hears it to sleep for three days and nights.

sources.book: Celtic Myth and Legend, Poetry and Romance

stories.title: Deirdre and the Sons of Usnech
stories.summary: Cathbad prophesies at Deirdre's birth that she will be beautiful beyond measure and that Ulster will be torn apart over her. The warriors want her killed; Conchobar keeps her instead, raised apart, to be his own wife. She sees a raven drinking a calf's blood on snow and says she would love a man with hair like the raven, cheek like the blood and body like the snow. That is Naoise. She corners him and forces the matter, and they flee to Scotland with his brothers. Conchobar lures them home under Fergus's guarantee of safety, detains Fergus by a contrived obligation, and has the sons of Usnech killed. Fergus goes into exile with three thousand men, and Deirdre dies by her own hand.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Boyhood Deeds of Cu Chulainn
stories.summary: Setanta walks to Emain Macha alone as a small boy, joins the boy-troop uninvited and beats all hundred and fifty of them at once. Invited to the smith Culann's house, he arrives late, is attacked by the guard hound and kills it - either by driving a ball down its throat or by dashing it against a stone - and, seeing the smith's grief, offers to guard the house himself until a pup can be reared. From that he takes the name Cu Chulainn, the hound of Culann. Later he overhears Cathbad telling a pupil that whoever takes up arms that day will be famous forever and live a short life, and goes straight to the king to ask for weapons, breaking fifteen sets before he is given the king's own.

sources.book: The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (Tain Bo Cuailnge)

stories.title: The Pillow Talk
stories.summary: Medb and Ailill lie in bed at Cruachan comparing what each brought to the marriage, and everything matches - the vessels, the jewels, the flocks, the horses - until they come to the herds, where Ailill has the white-horned bull Finnbhennach, which was calved in Medb's herd and left it because it would not be the property of a woman. She will not be one bull short of her husband. Told there is an equal in Ulster, the brown bull of Cuailnge, she offers its owner terms, and loses them when her messengers get drunk and boast that they would have taken it by force anyway. So she raises the armies of Ireland, with the exiled Fergus to guide them, and goes to fetch it.

sources.book: The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (Tain Bo Cuailnge)

stories.title: The Fights at the Ford
stories.summary: Macha's curse falls on the men of Ulster at the hour of their greatest need, and every warrior lies helpless with the pains of a woman in labour. Cu Chulainn, exempt, invokes the rule of single combat at a ford and holds the whole army of Ireland one champion at a time, through the winter. Medb sends warrior after warrior and offers her daughter Finnabair to each as a fee, and then offers her to several at once. The Morrigan attacks him in the water as an eel, a wolf and a red heifer and he wounds her each time; she returns as an old woman milking a cow with three teats, and he blesses her three times without knowing her, and heals all three wounds.

sources.book: The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (Tain Bo Cuailnge)

stories.title: Cu Chulainn and Ferdiad
stories.summary: Medb needs someone who can hold Cu Chulainn and comes at last to Ferdiad, his foster-brother, who trained beside him under Scathach. He refuses. She offers lands, and her daughter, and then the thing that moves him: that her poets will satirise him for cowardice, which would end his standing entirely. He goes. They fight three days at the ford, and each evening they stop, embrace, share food, and send healing herbs across the water to one another. On the fourth day Cu Chulainn is losing and calls for the Gae Bolg, which is thrown with the foot and opens into barbs inside the body. Afterwards he collapses across Ferdiad and laments that it had all been a game and a sport until Ferdiad came.

sources.book: The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (Tain Bo Cuailnge)

stories.title: The Two Bulls
stories.summary: The brown bull is taken and the armies disengage, and the war is settled by the animals it was fought over. The two bulls were once swineherds of rival lords who quarrelled and fought each other through successive forms - as ravens, as water creatures, as stags, as champions, as demons, as maggots - until each was swallowed by a cow and born as a bull. They meet at Cruachan and fight the length of Ireland for a day and a night. The Donn wins, and scatters pieces of the white bull across the country, leaving place-names behind it. Then it turns for home, and its heart bursts, and it dies. Nobody has gained anything at all, which is the ending the Tain chooses.

sources.book: The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (Tain Bo Cuailnge)

stories.title: Bricriu's Feast and the Beheading Game
stories.summary: Bricriu builds a hall with a balcony to watch from, invites all Ulster, and is told he may not stay because he cannot be trusted. On his way out he tells Loegaire, then Conall, then Cu Chulainn separately that the champion's portion belongs to him. The resulting quarrel runs the length of the story through several inconclusive judgements, until a monstrous churl walks in with an axe and offers his head to any man who will let him take theirs the following night. Cu Chulainn strikes; the churl picks up his head and leaves. Only Cu Chulainn returns to keep the bargain and lays his neck on the block. The churl is Cu Roi, and he names him first champion of Ireland. The same story reappears as Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

stories.title: The Death of Cu Chulainn
stories.summary: Cu Chulainn is bound by two contradictory prohibitions: never to refuse hospitality, and never to eat dog. Three hags roasting a hound on rowan spits offer him some, and whichever he does he breaks one. He eats, and his strength goes out of his spear hand. Wounded in the fighting that follows, with his charioteer and his horses dead, he ties himself upright to a standing stone with his own belt so that he will die on his feet, and the enemy do not dare approach for three days until a crow settles on his shoulder. Conall Cernach, bound by an old oath, hunts down everyone involved, giving up the use of one hand to fight a one-handed man fairly, and brings back the heads.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Salmon of Knowledge
stories.summary: Over the well of Segais at the head of the Boyne hang nine hazel trees, and their nuts fall into the water and are eaten by the salmon there, so that the wisdom in them passes into the fish. The poet Finn Eces has fished for it for seven years, having been told that he will catch it. He does, and sets the boy Fionn to cook it with instructions to eat none. Fat blisters on the skin and Fionn presses it with his thumb and burns himself, and puts the thumb in his mouth. The poet sees the knowledge in his face when he brings it, asks whether he ate any, and on hearing what happened gives him the whole fish. Ever afterwards Fionn has only to bite that thumb to know whatever he needs.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne
stories.summary: Grainne, promised to the ageing Fionn, sees the love spot on Diarmuid's forehead at her own betrothal feast, drugs the hall, and puts him under a binding he cannot refuse without disgrace: to take her away. He goes unwilling, out of obligation rather than desire, and they are hunted across Ireland for sixteen years, sleeping in a different place each night - the dolmens are still called their beds. Peace is eventually made and they live quietly. Then Fionn takes Diarmuid hunting the boar of Ben Bulben, which he is forbidden by geis to hunt, and he is gored. Fionn can heal any man with water carried in his hands, and twice he lets it run out through his fingers, and the third time he is too late.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: Oisin in Tir na nOg
stories.summary: Niamh of the Golden Hair rides out of the sea on a white horse and asks for Oisin by name, and takes him to Tir na nOg, where nobody ages or sickens. They are happy for what he takes to be three years, and then he wants to see his father and the Fianna again. She gives him the horse and one condition, telling him plainly what will happen: he must not let his foot touch Irish soil. He finds the Fianna three centuries gone and the country Christian, and stooping from the saddle to help some men shift a stone, his girth breaks. He touches the ground and becomes instantly, impossibly old. He spends what is left of his life telling the stories to Saint Patrick, and arguing with him about where the Fianna are now.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel
stories.summary: Conaire Mor is given a list of prohibitions at his making: never to go right-hand-wise round Tara, never to hunt the beasts of Cerna, never to let three red men go before him into a red man's house, and several more. His reign is famously good. Then his foster-brothers take to raiding, and rather than execute them he exiles them - and that mercy starts it. On a single day, forced by circumstance, he breaks each prohibition in turn, and ends besieged at Da Derga's hostel with three red men having ridden in ahead of him. In the middle of the fighting he dies of thirst, because every river and lake in Ireland has hidden itself from the man carrying his cup. It is the most tightly built tragedy in Irish literature.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: Niall and the Hag at the Well
stories.summary: Niall and his four half-brothers, out hunting, grow thirsty and find a well guarded by a woman described in the ugliest terms the text can manage - black-jointed, bristled, green-toothed. She will give water only in exchange for a kiss. Three refuse outright. One gives her the barest peck and gets a little water. Niall kisses her properly and lies with her, and she becomes the most beautiful woman in the world and tells him that she is Sovereignty, and that as she was first hideous and then lovely, so kingship is won by hard fighting before it becomes fair. His descendants held the high kingship for six centuries. The same story is told in English as the Wife of Bath's Tale.

sources.book: Myths and Legends of the Celtic Race

stories.title: Pwyll and the Lord of Annwn
stories.summary: Pwyll drives another man's hounds off a stag they have brought down, and the man is Arawn, king of Annwn. To make amends he agrees to exchange shapes and kingdoms for a year, and to kill Arawn's rival Hafgan at the end of it with a single blow, refusing to strike a second. What makes the story is what happens in between: he shares a bed with Arawn's wife every night for the year and turns his face to the wall each time without explanation, and when Arawn learns of it their friendship is permanent. Afterwards Pwyll sits on the mound at Arberth and sees a woman on a white horse riding at a walk whom no rider can overtake, until he thinks to ask her to stop.

stories.title: Branwen and the Cauldron
stories.summary: Branwen is married to the king of Ireland to bind the two islands, and her half-brother Efnysien, insulted at not being consulted, mutilates the Irish horses. Compensation is paid, including the cauldron that returns dead men to life without the power of speech, but the shame is not forgotten, and in Ireland Branwen is put out of the chamber, set to work in the kitchen and struck daily. She rears a starling on the rim of her kneading trough, teaches it to speak, and sends it to her brother. Bran wades the sea with an army and lies across the river as a bridge. The war ruins both islands: seven men survive in Britain, five pregnant women in Ireland, and Branwen's heart breaks looking at what she caused.

stories.title: The Woman Made of Flowers
stories.summary: Arianrhod, humiliated by a virginity test in open court, swears three destinies on the child that results: he shall have no name unless she names him, no arms unless she arms him, and no wife of any race on this earth. Gwydion defeats each by disguise and trickery, and for the third he and Math take the flowers of the oak, the broom and the meadowsweet and make a woman. Nobody asks her anything. She meets Gronw Pebr, and together they get from Lleu the absurdly elaborate conditions under which he can be killed, and arrange every one of them. Speared, he becomes an eagle; Gwydion finds him rotting in an oak and sings him down. Blodeuwedd is not killed but turned into an owl, shunned by every other bird.

stories.title: Ceridwen's Cauldron
stories.summary: Ceridwen's son is so ugly that she sets about brewing him all the knowledge in the world instead, a potion that must be stirred for a year and a day and yields three drops. She sets the boy Gwion Bach to stir it. At the end the three drops spit onto his thumb, he sucks it, and the knowledge is his - and the rest of the cauldron turns to poison and splits. She chases him: he becomes a hare and she a greyhound, a fish and she an otter, a bird and she a hawk, and at last a grain of wheat, and she a black hen, and eats him. Nine months later she bears him, cannot bring herself to kill him, and sets him adrift in a leather bag. He is found at a salmon weir and becomes Taliesin.

sources.book: Celtic Myth and Legend, Poetry and Romance

entities.name: Danu
entities.role: The mother of the Tuatha De Danann, known almost entirely from their name
symbols: the two hills called the Paps of Anu
entities.bio: A goddess reconstructed almost entirely backwards from a genitive in the name of her own children.
entities.longBio: Danu is the most important goddess in Irish mythology and very nearly the least attested. The Tuatha De Danann are the peoples of the goddess Danu, and from that phrase - plus a goddess Anu whom Cormac's Glossary calls the mother of the Irish gods, and two hills in Kerry called the Paps of Anu that look exactly like what they are named for - a mother goddess has been assembled. No story is told about her. She does nothing, says nothing and appears in no narrative. The nineteenth-century habit of connecting her to the Welsh Don and to the Danube and to Vedic Danu produced a great deal of confident writing that the evidence does not carry. She is included here because the pantheon is named after her, and the entry is honest that this is nearly all we have.
entities.variantTraditions: Some scholars read the name as Danann or Donann and doubt that a goddess Danu ever existed independently of the phrase. The identification with the Welsh Don is by position in the family tree rather than by any surviving story.

entities.name: The Dagda
entities.role: The Good God: not morally good, but good at everything
epithets: Ruad Rofhessa, lord of great knowledge
symbols: the club that kills with one end and revives with the other
the cauldron that is never empty
the harp that orders the seasons
entities.abode: Bruig na Boinne, until his son took it
entities.bio: The father-figure of the Tuatha De: a huge, coarse, enormously capable god with a club, a cauldron and a harp.
entities.longBio: The Dagda's title means the good god, and the sources are explicit that it means good at things rather than virtuous. He owns three treasures: a club so heavy it needs wheels, which kills with one end and restores life with the other; a cauldron from which no company ever went away unsatisfied; and a harp that calls the seasons into their order and the men of Ireland into laughter, grief or sleep. He is deliberately made ridiculous in Cath Maige Tuired - given a porridge pit to empty as a joke before the battle, he eats it with a ladle big enough to hold a man and a woman, and is left barely able to move. The same text has him mate with the Morrigan astride a river, and with a Fomorian woman, in both cases securing help for the coming fight. Comedy and cosmic authority sit in the same figure without embarrassment.
entities.variantTraditions: The comic treatment in Cath Maige Tuired may be Christian mockery of a pagan god, or may be genuinely old; the tone of the Irish sagas makes it hard to tell.

entities.name: Lugh
entities.role: Master of every art; the young god who takes command and kills his grandfather
epithets: Samildanach, skilled in all the arts together
entities.bio: Turned away at the gate for having no skill they lacked, until he asked whether anyone there had all of them.
entities.longBio: Lugh's arrival at Tara is the best-remembered scene in Irish mythology. The doorkeeper will not admit anyone without an art, so Lugh offers himself as wright, smith, champion, harper, warrior, poet, historian, sorcerer, physician, cupbearer and brazier, and each time is told they already have one. Then he asks whether they have any one man who is all of these at once, and the door opens. He takes command for the second battle of Moytura, and kills Balor, his own grandfather, with a sling-stone through the terrible eye. He is grandson of a Fomorian and son of a Tuatha De, and so belongs to both sides of the war he decides - which is the point rather than an accident. The harvest festival of Lughnasadh is his, held in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu, and it survives in Irish August fairs to this day.
entities.variantTraditions: The old identification of Lugh as a sun god comes from Victorian solar mythology and is not supported by the texts. His name is now generally connected to a root meaning oath or binding rather than light.

entities.name: Nuada
entities.role: King of the Tuatha De, who lost his hand and with it his right to rule
epithets: king of the Tuatha De Danann
entities.bio: A king unseated by a lost hand, restored by a silver one, and displaced again by a better man.
entities.longBio: Nuada leads the Tuatha De into Ireland and loses his hand in the first battle of Moytura against the Fir Bolg. Because Irish kingship requires a physically unblemished body, he must abdicate, and the crown passes to Bres, who proves a disaster. Dian Cecht makes him a working arm of silver, and Miach later grows flesh over it, and he is restored. But when Lugh arrives and demonstrates that he can do everything, Nuada gives up his seat voluntarily, which is a rare piece of good judgement in this literature. He is killed by Balor at the second battle. His silver arm and the requirement of wholeness make one of the clearest statements of the Irish rule that the king's body and the kingdom's health are the same thing.
entities.variantTraditions: The name is cognate with the British Nodens, worshipped at a temple at Lydney, and with the Welsh Nudd; the connection is linguistically secure even though no shared story survives.

entities.name: Brigid
entities.role: Poetry, smithcraft and healing in one goddess, who became a saint
entities.bio: A goddess of poetry, the forge and healing who was absorbed so completely into a Christian saint that the two cannot now be separated.
entities.longBio: Cormac's Glossary describes Brigid as a poet worshipped by poets, with two sisters of the same name, one a smith and one a healer - a triple goddess whose three faces cover exactly the skills a society most needed and most feared. She is the Dagda's daughter and Bres's wife, and it is her keening over her son Ruadan, killed at Moytura, that the sources call the first lament heard in Ireland. What happened to her afterwards is remarkable. Saint Brigid of Kildare shares her name, her feast day at Imbolc on the first of February, her association with fire, cattle and healing, and a perpetual flame at Kildare tended by nineteen nuns that burned into the twelfth century. Whether the saint is a real woman who inherited the goddess's cult, or the goddess in a wimple, is genuinely unresolved.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between goddess and saint is one of the most argued questions in Irish studies. The safest statement is that the cult of the saint absorbed the material of the goddess, whatever historical woman may lie behind it.

entities.name: The Morrigan
entities.role: The phantom queen: war, prophecy, and the crow over the battlefield
symbols: the eel, the wolf and the heifer
entities.bio: A goddess of war and prophecy who is a single figure, a trio, and a shape a crow takes, depending on the text.
entities.longBio: The Morrigan is not a goddess of fighting so much as of the fate that fighting delivers. She appears before battles to declare their outcome, and afterwards as a crow on the dead. Her name is read as either phantom queen or great queen and the sources disagree; so do they on whether she is one goddess or three, since Badb, Macha and Nemain are sometimes her sisters, sometimes her aspects, sometimes the whole of her. She mates with the Dagda astride the river Unius at Samhain and afterwards tells him where the Fomorians will land. Her long antagonism with Cu Chulainn is the finest thing in her record: she offers herself to him, he refuses her curtly, and she attacks him at the ford as an eel, a wolf and a red heifer in turn. He wounds her each time. She then appears as an old woman milking a cow with three teats, and he blesses her without knowing her, healing all three wounds.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether the Morrigan is a sovereignty goddess who turns to war, or a war goddess who acquires sovereignty language, is disputed. The trio Badb, Macha and Nemain is not stable across texts.

entities.name: Badb
entities.role: The crow of battle, whose cry decides which side breaks
symbols: the ford where armour is washed
entities.bio: The war goddess as panic itself: a crow screaming over the ranks, and a woman washing the armour of men about to die.
entities.longBio: Badb means crow, and specifically the hooded crow that follows armies. Her function is not to fight but to terrify - she shrieks over the host and men lose their nerve, which is a precise piece of observation about how ancient battles were actually decided. She is the most consistently attested of the war trio and outlasts the others, surviving into modern Irish folklore as the bean nighe or washer at the ford, seen scrubbing bloody clothes in a stream by a man who then recognises his own. At the end of Cath Maige Tuired it is Badb who speaks the two prophecies that close the text: first a vision of peace and plenty, then a terrible one of a world grown old, where summer is flowerless and the sea has no fish and old men speak lies.
entities.variantTraditions: The prophecy of the world's decay at the end of Moytura has been compared to Norse Ragnarok material; whether it reflects a native tradition or Christian apocalyptic is argued.

entities.name: Macha
entities.role: Sovereignty, horses and the curse that crippled Ulster
entities.bio: Forced to race a king's horses while heavily pregnant, she won, gave birth, and cursed the men of Ulster for nine generations.
entities.longBio: There are at least three Machas in the sources and they may or may not be the same. The one that matters most is the woman who comes to the farmer Crunnchu, brings him prosperity, and asks only that he say nothing about her. At the assembly he boasts that his wife can outrun the king's chariot horses. She is fetched, heavily pregnant, and begs for a delay until she has given birth; the king refuses and the crowd insists. She runs, wins, gives birth to twins at the finish - which is what Emain Macha means - and dies, cursing the men of Ulster to suffer the pains of a woman in labour for five days and four nights at their hour of greatest need, for nine generations. That curse is the mechanism of the entire Tain: when Medb invades, every Ulsterman is on the ground, and only Cu Chulainn, exempt because he is not of Ulster's blood, can stand.
entities.variantTraditions: The three Machas - wife of Nemed, the red-haired queen, and Crunnchu's wife - are treated as one goddess by some scholars and as separate figures by others.

entities.name: Nemain
entities.role: Frenzy: the confusion that makes armies kill their own
symbols: the scream heard over the host
entities.bio: The least individual of the war goddesses and the most specific in effect: she is the noise that makes an army destroy itself.
entities.longBio: Nemain is barely a character. She has no story of her own, and appears as a function - her cry raised over the ranks kills a hundred of Medb's men in a night from sheer terror in the Tain, and the text is clear they die of the sound rather than of any weapon. Her name is related to words for frenzy and venom. She is sometimes named as a wife of Net, an obscure war god, sometimes as one of the Morrigan's aspects, and sometimes conflated with Badb outright. She is included because the Irish war goddesses divide their work with unusual precision: Morrigan is the fate of the battle, Badb is the terror of it, Nemain is the disorder inside it, and together they describe defeat more exactly than a god of fighting ever could.
entities.variantTraditions: Nemain and Badb are treated as the same goddess in several sources, and the trio of war goddesses is not consistently named across texts.

entities.name: Ogma
entities.role: Champion of the Tuatha De and inventor of the ogham alphabet
symbols: the ogham strokes cut along a stone edge
entities.bio: The strong man of the Tuatha De, credited with inventing writing - and with binding men by the ears with chains from his tongue.
entities.longBio: Ogma is the champion, the one who throws the great flagstone and fights in the front line, and he is also the inventor of ogham, the alphabet of notches cut along the edge of a standing stone that is the earliest form of written Irish. That pairing of brute strength with eloquence is unusual and deliberate. The Greek writer Lucian, visiting Gaul in the second century, describes being shown a picture of a god the locals called Ogmios: an old man with a club and a lion skin, drawing a crowd of willing followers after him by fine gold chains running from his tongue to their ears. His guide explained that among the Gauls eloquence, not force, is what leads people. Whether Ogmios and Ogma are the same god is uncertain, but the coincidence of a strong man who is also the master of words is striking.
entities.variantTraditions: The connection between Irish Ogma and Gaulish Ogmios is widely assumed and linguistically awkward; the names do not correspond as neatly as they appear to.

entities.name: Dian Cecht
entities.role: Physician of the Tuatha De, who killed his son for being better at it
epithets: the leech of the Tuatha De
entities.bio: The god of healing, whose jealousy of his own son's greater skill is one of the ugliest stories in the cycle.
entities.longBio: Dian Cecht makes Nuada's silver arm, and with his children chants over the well of Slaine so that the dead of the Tuatha De thrown into it come out whole - a piece of battlefield logistics that the text presents matter-of-factly. But his son Miach goes further, growing real flesh and skin over Nuada's silver arm in nine days. Dian Cecht strikes him with a sword, three times cutting the skin and three times having it healed by his son, then splits his brain, which Miach cannot mend. From Miach's grave grow three hundred and sixty-five herbs, one for every joint and sinew in the body, and his sister Airmid gathers and arranges them on her cloak. Their father overturns the cloak and scatters them, and the text says that but for this, people would be immortal. The healing arts are lost out of a professional's envy.
entities.variantTraditions: The number of herbs varies between manuscripts, and the detail that people would otherwise not die is not in every copy.

entities.name: Miach
entities.role: The better physician, killed by his father, whose grave grew every healing herb
symbols: the three hundred and sixty-five herbs
entities.bio: He grew a real arm where his father had made a silver one, and was murdered for it.
entities.longBio: Miach and his sister Airmid find Nuada with the silver arm Dian Cecht made, and Miach says a real one would be better. He finds the buried original, sets it in place, chants over it, and in three nine-day stages joint knits to joint and sinew to sinew until the king has his own hand back. His father's response is to attack him with a sword four times, and the fourth blow, through the brain, is the one Miach cannot heal. He is a small figure with an outsized point: the Irish material is not sentimental about its gods, and the reason human beings are not immortal, in this tradition, is that one doctor could not stand being outdone by another.
entities.variantTraditions: Miach does not appear in every version of the Moytura material, and the herb story is sometimes told of Airmid alone.

entities.name: Airmid
entities.role: Herbalist who learned every healing plant, and lost the knowledge in an afternoon
symbols: the cloak spread with sorted herbs
entities.bio: She sorted the three hundred and sixty-five herbs on her cloak in the order of their uses, and her father scattered them.
entities.longBio: Airmid helps her brother regrow Nuada's arm and chants with her family over the well that restores the dead. Her own moment comes at Miach's grave, where three hundred and sixty-five herbs grow up through the earth, one for each joint and sinew of his body. She gathers them and lays them out on her cloak arranged by which part of the body each will cure - which is not merely collecting but the invention of a system, the first materia medica. Dian Cecht turns the cloak over and mixes them beyond recovery, and the knowledge is gone. The detail that survives is the arrangement rather than the herbs: what is lost is not the plants, which still grow, but the ordering of them. As an account of why medicine is difficult it is uncomfortably good.
entities.variantTraditions: Airmid's role is expanded in modern retellings well beyond what the medieval texts give her, which is a few sentences.

entities.name: Goibniu
entities.role: The smith, whose spearheads never missed and whose ale kept the gods from ageing
epithets: the smith of the Tuatha De
symbols: the three blows that finish a spear
entities.bio: One of the three craftsmen who kept the Tuatha De armed, and the host of a feast whose ale kept age and sickness away.
entities.longBio: Goibniu forms a working trio with Credne the metalworker and Luchta the wright. During the second battle they run what amounts to an arms factory just off the field: Goibniu makes a spearhead with three blows of the hammer, Luchta throws a shaft in three cuts, Credne casts the rivets, and the parts fly together without anyone joining them. Every weapon Goibniu makes finds its mark, and every wound it makes is fatal. A Fomorian spy called Ruadan is sent to kill him and wounds him with a spear the smith himself made; Goibniu pulls it out and throws it back, killing him. He also presides over the Fled Goibnenn, the feast of Goibniu, whose ale preserved the Tuatha De from age and decay - the closest thing in Irish myth to the food of the gods.
entities.variantTraditions: The name is from the Irish word for smith, and is cognate with the Welsh Gofannon; the two share a name and an occupation but no story.

entities.name: Credne
entities.role: The bronze-worker, who cast rivets faster than they could be fitted
epithets: the brazier of the Tuatha De
entities.bio: The third of the three craft gods, who supplied the fittings while the other two made the blades and shafts.
entities.longBio: Credne is a specialist in the non-ferrous metals - bronze, brass and gold - and his part in the wartime forge is the rivets, the ferrules and the fastenings that turn a head and a shaft into a spear. The image of the three craftsmen working in relay, with the finished parts springing together of their own accord, is one of the most vivid pieces of the Moytura text, and it is essentially an account of a production line. He also helps make Nuada's silver arm. Credne is a reminder that this pantheon takes craft very seriously indeed: three separate gods for what could have been one, distinguished by material and technique, in a society where metalworkers were both indispensable and slightly suspect.
entities.variantTraditions: Credne is drowned crossing to Ireland from Spain in one late tradition, which does not fit the Moytura material and is probably a separate figure.

entities.name: Luchta
entities.role: The wright, who cut a spear-shaft in three strokes and threw it to the smith
epithets: the wright of the Tuatha De
entities.bio: The carpenter of the trio, who made the shafts and the shields for the second battle of Moytura.
entities.longBio: Luchta completes the craft triad. He works wood: the shafts of spears, thrown to Goibniu so fast that they arrive as the heads are finished, and the shields the Tuatha De carry. Alongside the three of them, Cath Maige Tuired lists what every specialist will contribute before the battle - the smith, the wright, the brazier, the physician, the sorcerer, the cupbearers, the druid - each stating what they will do and how. It is one of the most distinctive passages in Irish literature and it reads less like a myth than a muster roll. The gods of this tradition are defined by what they can make and do, and a war is won by having better craftsmen than the other side.
entities.variantTraditions: The name is sometimes given as Luchtaine. He is otherwise unattested outside the Moytura material.

entities.name: Boann
entities.role: The river Boyne, who made it by walking round a forbidden well
entities.bio: She walked three times counterclockwise around a well she was forbidden to approach, and the water rose and pursued her to the sea.
entities.longBio: Boann is the wife of Nechtan, who keeps a well that no one may look into but himself and his cupbearers. She goes to it anyway - to prove her power, or to wash away a rumour, depending on the version - and walks three times widdershins around it. The water rises and bursts out after her, taking an eye, an arm and a thigh as she runs, and follows her all the way to the sea, becoming the river Boyne. Over the well hang nine hazel trees whose nuts fall into the water and are eaten by the salmon, and the wisdom of the nuts passes into the fish; anyone who eats such a salmon gets it too, which is how Fionn later acquires his knowledge. She is also the mother of Aengus by the Dagda, conceived and carried in a single day her husband did not notice.
entities.variantTraditions: The well is called Segais, and it also produces the Shannon in a nearly identical story about a woman called Sinann. The pattern of a river made by a woman transgressing at a well is a recognised Irish type.

entities.name: Aengus
entities.role: The young son: god of love, who won his home with a riddle about time
entities.abode: Bruig na Boinne, the passage tomb at Newgrange
entities.bio: Conceived and born in a day that was made to last nine months, he later used the same trick to take his father's house.
entities.longBio: The Dagda desires Boann, who is married to Nechtan, so he sends Nechtan away and holds the sun still for nine months, which pass as a single day; Aengus is conceived and born inside it. Grown, he asks the Dagda for the Bruig - the great passage tomb on the Boyne - for a day and a night, and when the time is up refuses to leave, arguing that all of time is days and nights and so the loan was permanent. He keeps it. His own love story is the finest thing attached to him: he dreams of a woman and sickens for want of her, and she is found after long searching to be Caer Ibormeith, who lives as a swan every second year with a hundred and fifty others, all chained in pairs. He picks her out, becomes a swan himself, and they fly away singing music that puts everyone who hears it to sleep for three days.
entities.variantTraditions: Bruig na Boinne is Newgrange, a real Neolithic passage tomb some three thousand years older than any of these stories. The Irish attached their gods to monuments they had inherited and could not explain.

entities.name: Midir
entities.role: Lord of Bri Leith, who won his wife back over a chessboard
entities.bio: He played a mortal king at board games for stakes he chose afterwards, lost on purpose, and then asked for a kiss from the queen.
entities.longBio: Midir's story is a long game. He loves Etain, whom his jealous first wife Fuamnach turns into a pool, a worm and then a fly, and blows away on a wind for a thousand years until she is swallowed by a mortal woman and reborn as a human, with no memory. She marries the High King Eochaid. Midir arrives and challenges Eochaid to fidchell, a board game, letting him win the first games and pay handsomely, then staking everything on the last - and when he wins he asks for his arms around Etain and a kiss. Eochaid delays a month and fills his fortress with armed men, and Midir simply appears in the middle of the hall, takes her, and the two leave through the roof as swans. What follows is Eochaid digging up sid mounds for a year to get her back, and being fooled with fifty identical women.
entities.variantTraditions: Tochmarc Etaine survives in fragments and the sequence of Etain's rebirths is reconstructed from more than one manuscript.

entities.name: Etain
entities.role: Transformed into a fly and blown on the wind for a thousand years, then reborn as a mortal
epithets: the most beautiful woman in Ireland
symbols: the cup she is swallowed in
entities.bio: Turned into water, a worm and a fly by a rival, blown about Ireland for a thousand years, swallowed in a drink and born again.
entities.longBio: Etain marries Midir, and his first wife Fuamnach strikes her with a rod of scarlet quicken and turns her into a pool of water, which becomes a worm, which becomes a purple fly of extraordinary beauty whose humming is sweeter than music. Midir knows the fly is her and carries it everywhere until Fuamnach raises a wind that blows it about Ireland for seven years without rest. It lands at last in a cup of a woman of Ulster, who swallows it and conceives, and Etain is born again as a mortal a thousand and twelve years after her first birth, with no memory of any of it. She grows up, is chosen by the High King, and is eventually recognised and reclaimed by the husband she cannot remember. The story is unusual in Irish literature for taking a woman's identity as its whole subject.
entities.variantTraditions: The name of the second Etain, her daughter, is confused with hers in the manuscripts, and Eochaid's unwitting incest in one version may be a scribal tangle rather than a plot point.

entities.name: Manannan mac Lir
entities.role: God of the sea, master of illusion, and keeper of the way to the Otherworld
epithets: the horseman of the crested waves
symbols: the boat Wave-sweeper that needs no oars
the horse Enbarr that runs on water
entities.abode: Emain Ablach, and the Isle of Man
entities.bio: The sea itself and the road across it: he lends heroes his horse, hides the Tuatha De in mist, and rules the island of apples.
entities.longBio: Manannan is not quite one of the Tuatha De and not quite outside them. He arrives when needed, usually by sea, and he owns almost every useful object in Irish myth: a boat that goes where its owner wishes without sail or oar, a horse that crosses water as easily as land, a sword called the Answerer, a cloak that he shakes between two lovers so they never meet again, and pigs that can be killed and eaten and are alive the next morning. After the Tuatha De are defeated by the Milesians, it is Manannan who assigns them their mounds and raises the feth fiada, the veil of mist that makes them invisible. He gives his name to the Isle of Man, where a tradition of paying him rent in rushes at midsummer survived for centuries.
entities.variantTraditions: Manannan is not listed among the Tuatha De in the earliest sources and may be a separate and older figure. The Welsh Manawydan shares his name and parentage but almost nothing else.

entities.name: Lir
entities.role: A sea god remembered almost entirely for the fate of his children
entities.bio: Overlooked for the kingship of the Tuatha De, and father of the four children turned to swans for nine hundred years.
entities.longBio: Lir is a shadowy figure whose importance is entirely inherited: he is the father of Manannan, and the father of the four children in one of the three sorrowful tales of Ireland. When Bodb Derg is chosen king of the Tuatha De over him he takes it badly, and is reconciled by being given Bodb's daughter Aeb in marriage. She bears four children and dies, and her sister Aoife, who takes her place, grows jealous of the love Lir bears them. She takes them to a lake and strikes them with a druid's wand into four white swans, leaving them their voices and their reason, for nine hundred years: three hundred on Lake Derravaragh, three hundred on the Sea of Moyle, three hundred at Erris. Lir finds them and can do nothing but come to the shore to listen to them singing.
entities.variantTraditions: The Fate of the Children of Lir is a late composition, probably fifteenth or sixteenth century, and its Christian ending - the swans restored as ancient people who are baptised and die - is integral rather than added.

entities.name: Fand
entities.role: Otherworld queen who took Cu Chulainn as a lover and gave him up
entities.abode: Mag Mell, the plain of delight
entities.bio: Abandoned by Manannan, she summoned Cu Chulainn to her country, loved him, and then let him go rather than see his wife suffer.
entities.longBio: Fand is Manannan's wife, left by him, and she sends birds and then a summons to Cu Chulainn to come to her country and fight her enemies. He goes, wins, and stays a month. When he returns and continues to meet her, his wife Emer comes with fifty women armed with knives, and there follows one of the most surprising conversations in Irish literature: Emer argues that what is old and familiar is honoured, Cu Chulainn says he has always found Emer fine and will again, and Fand, watching, decides to give him up. Manannan comes at her call, and she goes back to him because, she says, he has no other woman worthy of him, while Cu Chulainn has. Manannan then shakes his cloak between Fand and Cu Chulainn so that they can never meet again, and the hero is given a drink of forgetting.
entities.variantTraditions: Serglige Con Culainn survives in a manuscript that appears to combine two versions, and the text itself notes a conflict between them.

entities.name: Bodb Derg
entities.role: Chosen king of the Tuatha De after the Milesians took the land above
epithets: king of the sidhe of Munster
entities.bio: Elected to rule the Tuatha De in their mounds after the defeat, and the one who searched Ireland for Aengus's dream-woman.
entities.longBio: When the Tuatha De are driven under the ground they hold an election, and Bodb Derg, a son of the Dagda, is chosen over Lir. He rules from a mound in Munster and is the figure the others come to when something must be adjudicated or found. It is Bodb who spends a year searching Ireland for the woman Aengus has only seen in dreams, and locates her at last on a lake with a hundred and fifty swans. It is Bodb's daughters whom Lir marries, and Bodb who punishes Aoife for turning his grandchildren into swans by transforming her into a demon of the air forever. He represents something the Irish material does unusually well: a defeated people continuing to govern themselves in exile, with elections, lawsuits and grievances intact.
entities.variantTraditions: His epithet derg, red, is unexplained. He is sometimes confused with the war goddess Badb in later sources on the strength of the similar name.

entities.name: Balor
entities.role: The Fomorian with the eye that kills whatever it looks at
symbols: the four men who lift the lid with a ring
entities.bio: One eye that withered an army when it opened, and a prophecy that his grandson would kill him.
entities.longBio: Balor's eye was poisoned as a boy when he looked in on his father's druids brewing spells and the fumes got into it. It is kept closed by a lid so heavy that four men are needed to raise it with a polished ring, and whatever it falls on dies. Told by a druid that his own grandson would kill him, he locks his only daughter Ethniu in a tower on Tory Island so she will never meet a man. Cian gets in, and Lugh is born. At the second battle of Moytura the lid is levered up and the eye begins to open, and Lugh puts a sling-stone through it, driving the eye out through the back of Balor's head so that it kills his own army behind him. The grandfather-killing prophecy, the tower, the impossible confinement - it is the same shape as Perseus and Acrisius, and nobody has satisfactorily explained why.
entities.variantTraditions: In folklore Balor is killed with a red-hot iron rod rather than a sling-stone, and survives all over the Donegal coast in place-names. The Perseus parallel is noted by every commentator and explained by none.

entities.name: Bres
entities.role: The beautiful king whose meanness cost him the throne
entities.bio: Made king because he was handsome and half-Fomorian, deposed because he was stingy - which in Ireland is a disqualifying offence.
entities.longBio: With Nuada unfit to rule after losing his hand, the Tuatha De make Bres king because he is beautiful and because his Fomorian father might keep the peace. He turns out to be a catastrophe, and the specific charge is not cruelty but meanness: he taxes the Tuatha De into servitude, puts the Dagda to digging ditches and Ogma to carrying firewood, and above all he does not entertain. The text says the knives of his household were never greased and the breath of his people never smelled of ale. When the poet Cairbre visits and is given a small dry room with no fire, no bed and three dry cakes, he composes the first satire ever made in Ireland, and blisters break out on Bres's face. A blemished king cannot rule, so the satire deposes him. He flees to the Fomorians and brings back an army.
entities.variantTraditions: Bres is spared at the end of Moytura in exchange for teaching the Tuatha De when to plough, sow and reap, which turns a war story into an agricultural one at the last moment.

entities.name: Elatha
entities.role: Fomorian prince who came by sea in a silver boat and fathered Bres
entities.bio: A Fomorian who is described as beautiful rather than monstrous, which complicates the whole idea of what the Fomorians were.
entities.longBio: Eriu is alone by the sea when a silver boat comes in and a man steps out with golden hair to his shoulders and gold ornaments, and the text says she thought him the most beautiful thing she had ever seen. He lies with her, leaves her a gold ring, and tells her the son will be called Eochu Bres. That son becomes the ruinous king. Elatha matters because he ruins the neat reading of the Fomorians as monsters or chaos - he is a king across the water, handsome and courteous, and when Bres comes to him for an army after being deposed he tells his son plainly that it is not right to win by injustice what he could not hold by justice. The Fomorians in the earliest material are more like a rival aristocracy than demons.
entities.variantTraditions: The later tradition of the Fomorians as one-legged, one-armed monsters is largely from the Lebor Gabala and folk material, and sits awkwardly beside portraits like this one.

entities.name: Ethniu
entities.role: Balor's daughter, locked in a tower, who became Lugh's mother
entities.bio: Imprisoned so that the prophecy about her son could not come true, which is precisely how it came true.
entities.longBio: Balor is told his grandson will kill him, so he shuts his only daughter in a tower on Tory Island with twelve women to attend her, and no man is to be spoken of in her hearing. Cian, whose magical cow Balor has stolen, gets to the island - by a druid's help, or dressed as a woman, depending on the version - and Ethniu bears a son, or in the folk versions triplets, whom Balor orders drowned. One survives. That child is Lugh, and he kills Balor at Moytura. Ethniu herself is given almost nothing to say in any version, which is a fair summary of how the tradition treats her: she is the mechanism by which a prophecy defeats the man trying to prevent it, and the story shows no interest in what she wanted.
entities.variantTraditions: The folk versions differ considerably from the medieval text, and the drowned-triplets motif is largely oral tradition from Donegal.

entities.name: Cian
entities.role: Lugh's father, murdered by three brothers who were made to pay impossibly for it
epithets: the owner of the Glas Gaibhnenn
entities.bio: He reached Balor's daughter in her tower, and was later killed in pig form by the sons of Tuireann.
entities.longBio: Cian owns the Glas Gaibhnenn, a cow whose milk never fails, and when Balor steals her he goes to Tory Island after her and gets to Ethniu. Lugh is the result. Cian's own end comes when he meets the three sons of Tuireann, with whom his family is at feud, and turns himself into a pig to hide in a herd. They spot him, wound him, and he asks to be allowed to return to human shape first so he can be killed as a man - which they grant, and he tells them they have now made themselves liable for the killing of a man rather than a pig, which is a far greater price. They stone him to death and the earth refuses his body six times. Lugh, told of it, sets them a blood-fine consisting of eight impossible tasks, and they complete all of them and die of it.
entities.variantTraditions: The Fate of the Children of Tuireann is one of the three sorrowful tales of Ireland, and survives mainly in late and elaborated versions.

entities.name: Indech
entities.role: Fomorian king who fell at Moytura
symbols: the war host from the sea
entities.bio: One of the Fomorian kings at the second battle, killed by Ogma, whose own death came in the same fight.
entities.longBio: Indech son of Domnu leads the Fomorians alongside Balor and Bres. Before the battle he is one of those the Morrigan and the Dagda's intelligence-gathering is directed against, and the Dagda meets and sleeps with his daughter, who promises to turn her magic against her own people. In the fighting Indech and Ogma kill one another, and the text records it in the flat, list-making way that these battle accounts favour - a catalogue of who fell to whom, without comment. He is a reminder that the Fomorians have a genuine command structure with several kings rather than a single dark lord, and that the war is presented as a war between peoples rather than between good and evil.
entities.variantTraditions: The patronymic mac De Domnann, son of the goddess Domnu, is one of the few traces of a Fomorian mother-goddess.

entities.name: Tethra
entities.role: Fomorian king whose sword told everything it had done
epithets: lord of Mag Mell in later tradition
entities.abode: Beyond the sea, and Mag Mell
entities.bio: Killed at Moytura, after which Ogma took his sword and it recited every deed it had done.
entities.longBio: Tethra falls at the second battle, and Ogma takes his sword Orna from the field. When it is unsheathed and cleaned it speaks, reciting all the deeds that had been done with it - a small, strange detail the text explains by saying that swords in those days used to talk, and that this is why they were regarded as demons. Tethra is afterwards associated with the Otherworld: fish are called the cattle of Tethra, and in some poems the dead go to his plain. That drift from a defeated enemy king to a lord of the country of the dead is very characteristic of this material, where the losing side does not disappear but relocates.
entities.variantTraditions: The identification of Tethra's realm with Mag Mell is late, and may be a poetic flourish rather than a real tradition.

entities.name: Cethlenn
entities.role: Balor's wife, a prophetess who wounded the Dagda
symbols: the spear or dart she threw
entities.bio: She foresaw the Fomorian defeat, warned her husband, and gave the Dagda the wound he eventually died of.
entities.longBio: Cethlenn is Balor's wife and a prophetess, and it is she who warns him that Lugh's arrival among the Tuatha De means the end of Fomorian power. At Moytura she wounds the Dagda - the great god of the Tuatha De, who does not die then but is said in some accounts to die of it eighty years later, which is a very Irish way of handling the death of a god. Her name is preserved in Enniskillen, Inis Ceithleann, the island of Cethlenn, in County Fermanagh. She is one of several figures in this cycle who see clearly what is coming and are on the losing side anyway, which the literature treats as ordinary rather than tragic.
entities.variantTraditions: The tradition that the Dagda died of Cethlenn's wound appears in some annals and not in the Moytura text itself.

entities.name: Cesair
entities.role: Leader of the first people to reach Ireland, forty days before the Flood
epithets: the first to come to Ireland
symbols: the fifty women and three men
entities.bio: She arrived with fifty women and three men, in a scheme that failed on arithmetic and then on the Flood.
entities.longBio: The Lebor Gabala begins with Cesair, who in the Christianising scheme is Noah's granddaughter, refused a place on the Ark and told to sail west to a land no one has ever sinned in. Three ships set out and one arrives, with fifty women and three men. They divide the women between the men; two of the men die, and Fintan, faced with what remains, flees and turns himself into a salmon. Cesair dies of grief and the Flood arrives forty days after their landing and drowns them all except Fintan. The whole episode is transparently a monkish invention, constructed to give Ireland a history that starts from Noah, and it is included here for exactly that reason: it shows the machinery of the tradition working in plain sight.
entities.variantTraditions: Cesair has no plausible pre-Christian origin. She is a literary construct of the Lebor Gabala compilers, and the text itself admits uncertainty about where the story came from.

entities.name: Partholon
entities.role: Leader of the second invasion, whose people all died of plague in a week
entities.bio: His people cleared plains, brewed the first ale and fought the Fomorians - and then died of plague in a single week, all five thousand of them.
entities.longBio: Partholon arrives after the Flood and his people begin the work of making Ireland habitable: four plains are cleared, seven lakes burst forth, cattle are herded, the first ale is brewed, the first guest-house built, the first jealousy and the first adultery occur. They fight the Fomorians, who are already there and are always already there. Then plague takes all of them in one week, and they are buried together on a plain outside what is now Dublin. Only Tuan, Partholon's nephew, survives, and he does so by shapeshifting through several animal forms for centuries. The pattern - arrival, clearing, achievement, total extinction, one survivor to tell it - repeats through the invasions, and is the frame the whole pseudo-history hangs on.
entities.variantTraditions: The invasion sequence is a medieval synthetic history rather than surviving mythology, though it may incorporate older material about the Fomorians and the Tuatha De.

entities.name: Nemed
entities.role: Leader of the third invasion, whose survivors became the Fir Bolg and the Tuatha De
entities.bio: His people were ground down by Fomorian tribute, stormed a tower, lost almost everyone, and scattered - and their descendants came back as the next two invasions.
entities.longBio: Nemed's people arrive and are subjected by the Fomorians to a tribute so severe it has become the standard Irish image of oppression: two thirds of their children, their corn and their milk, delivered every Samhain to Conand's tower on Tory Island. They rise, storm the tower and kill Conand, but a Fomorian fleet arrives and in the battle the sea rises and nearly all of both sides drown. Thirty survivors scatter - some to Greece, some to the north of the world - and their descendants return as the Fir Bolg and as the Tuatha De Danann. This is the joint that holds the whole pseudo-history together, and it is doing a lot of work: it makes the gods and the Fir Bolg relatives, and it makes the Fomorian tribute the original grievance.
entities.variantTraditions: The tribute of two thirds of the children is echoed in later Irish complaints about foreign rule and may have been shaped by them.

entities.name: The Fir Bolg
entities.role: The fourth people to hold Ireland, defeated by the Tuatha De at the first Moytura
domains: the division of Ireland into five provinces
entities.abode: Ireland, and afterwards the western islands
entities.bio: They divided Ireland into its five provinces, then lost it to the Tuatha De in a fair fight with agreed rules.
entities.longBio: The Fir Bolg are descendants of Nemed's scattered people, said to have been enslaved in Greece carrying earth in leather bags, from which their name is derived - a folk etymology that is almost certainly wrong. They hold Ireland for thirty-seven years and their real contribution is administrative: they divide the island into the five provinces that Ireland still recognises, and establish kingship. When the Tuatha De arrive they meet at the first battle of Moytura, which is fought with unusual formality - envoys, agreed weapons, and a request from the Fir Bolg for time to make spears as light as the Tuatha De's. They lose, their king Eochaid mac Eirc is killed, and the survivors are given Connacht. They are not demonised, which stands out.
entities.variantTraditions: Some scholars connect the Fir Bolg to the historical Builg or Belgae, making them the one invasion with a possible real-world referent.

entities.name: Tuan mac Cairill
entities.role: The one survivor of Partholon's people, who lived through every invasion as a series of animals
epithets: the old man of the ages
symbols: the stag, the boar, the hawk, the salmon
entities.abode: Ireland, in every age of it
entities.bio: He outlived his people by becoming a stag, then a boar, then a hawk, then a salmon - and was eaten, and reborn as a man who remembered it all.
entities.longBio: Tuan survives the plague that kills Partholon's people and lives alone, ageing, until he is renewed as a young stag and runs with the deer through Nemed's time. He becomes a boar, then a hawk - watching the Fir Bolg and the Tuatha De arrive from the air - then a salmon, and as a salmon he is caught and eaten by the wife of Cairell, and is born again as her son with every memory intact. In the sixth century he tells the whole of it to Saint Finnian. The device is doing something clever: it gives the pseudo-history an eyewitness, and it converts a pagan account into legitimate testimony by having it delivered to a saint. Fintan mac Bochra does the same job in a parallel text, which suggests the monks liked the solution.
entities.variantTraditions: Tuan and Fintan are near-duplicates, and the two texts appear to be competing versions of the same idea rather than one tradition.

entities.name: Fintan mac Bochra
entities.role: The salmon of knowledge in human form: he saw everything and told it
entities.bio: The one man who escaped the Flood in Ireland, by turning into a salmon and hiding in a cave for a year.
entities.longBio: Fintan arrives with Cesair, flees the arrangement he finds himself in, and survives the Flood as a salmon under a cave at Tul Tuinde. He lives five thousand years through every invasion, taking the shapes of an eagle, a hawk and a salmon, and in the end is summoned to settle a question no one else can answer: how Ireland should properly be divided, and what belongs to each of the five provinces. He answers from memory, because he was there. In one late and lovely poem he holds a conversation with the Hawk of Achill, the two of them the oldest living things, comparing what they have seen. Fintan is the Irish tradition thinking about its own transmission: someone must have remembered all this, so a man is invented who could.
entities.variantTraditions: The Fintan and Tuan traditions overlap heavily and are probably variants. The dialogue with the Hawk of Achill is a late medieval composition.

entities.name: Eriu
entities.role: The sovereignty goddess whose name Ireland still carries
entities.bio: One of three sisters who each asked the invaders to name the island after her; hers is the name that stuck.
entities.longBio: When the Milesians land, they meet three goddesses in turn - Banba, Fodla and Eriu - each of whom asks that the island be named for her. Amergin the poet promises each of them. Eriu's is the name that survives: Eire, and in the genitive Erenn, and eventually Ireland. She is married to Mac Greine, one of the three kings of the Tuatha De who are ruling jointly at the time, and she is not simply a namesake but the land as a person - a king takes the sovereignty by union with her, and the standard image is a woman offering a cup. That is the underlying logic of a great deal of Irish kingship material, and it explains why the land fails when a king is unjust: the marriage has gone wrong.
entities.variantTraditions: Eriu is also given a Fomorian father, Elatha, in one tradition, making the sovereignty of Ireland half-Fomorian - a detail that complicates any reading of the Fomorians as simply the enemy.

entities.name: Banba
entities.role: One of the three sovereignty sisters; a poetic name for Ireland
entities.bio: The first of the three sisters to meet the Milesians, and a name for Ireland still used in poetry.
entities.longBio: Banba meets the invaders first, on the mountain called Slieve Mish, and asks that her name be given to the island. Amergin agrees. Her name did not become the ordinary one but survived as a poetic and literary name for Ireland, used in bardic verse for centuries in the way Albion is used for Britain. She is the wife of Mac Cuill, one of the three joint kings of the Tuatha De. The three sisters make one goddess in three, or three goddesses of one land, and the tradition does not choose. In some accounts Banba is also the leader of the very first settlement, before Cesair, which suggests she was an older figure who was later fitted into the invasion scheme.
entities.variantTraditions: The tradition that Banba, rather than Cesair, led the first settlement appears in some recensions of the Lebor Gabala and is probably the older version.

entities.name: Fodla
entities.role: The third sovereignty sister; another poetic name for the island
entities.bio: The third of the sisters, whose name also survives as a literary name for Ireland.
entities.longBio: Fodla makes the same request as her sisters and receives the same promise. Like Banba she survives as a poetic name for Ireland rather than the common one. Her husband is Mac Cecht, the third of the joint kings. The three sisters are the clearest surviving statement of Irish sovereignty theology: the land is a woman, she has three names and three faces, and a people takes possession by making an agreement with her rather than simply by winning. Amergin's promise to all three, and his keeping of it by giving Ireland all three names in different registers, is the sort of legal precision the Irish material enjoys - the bargain is honoured to the letter.
entities.variantTraditions: The trio of Eriu, Banba and Fodla is often read as a triple goddess of the same kind as the Morrigan's trio, though the two groups never overlap in the texts.

entities.name: Amergin
entities.role: The Milesian poet who judged the taking of Ireland and spoke the first poem in it
domains: the law of the taking of land
symbols: the foot set on Irish soil
entities.bio: He ruled that his own people must withdraw beyond the ninth wave and win the land back fairly, and then sang the land into their hands.
entities.longBio: When the Milesians land, the three kings of the Tuatha De ask for a judgement, and Amergin - who is on the invading side - rules against his own people: they must return to their ships, go out beyond the ninth wave, and land again, giving the Tuatha De a fair chance to prevent them. The text calls this the first judgement given in Ireland. The Tuatha De raise a druidic storm that scatters the fleet and drowns several of his brothers. Amergin answers it with a poem, and as he sets his right foot on the shore he speaks the verse that begins I am the wind on the sea - a chain of identifications with the elements, the stag, the hawk, the salmon, the word. It is the most famous poem in Irish and its date and meaning are both fiercely argued.
entities.variantTraditions: The Song of Amergin survives in versions differing considerably, and the familiar English text owes a good deal to nineteenth-century translators. Comparisons with the Bhagavad Gita are common and rest on very little.

entities.name: Mil Espaine
entities.role: Ancestor of the Gaels, who never reached Ireland himself
symbols: the tower in Spain from which Ireland was seen
entities.bio: The Gaels are named for a man who died before the voyage - his sons took Ireland to avenge an uncle killed there.
entities.longBio: Mil Espaine is a construction, and a visible one: the name is Miles Hispaniae, the soldier of Spain, lifted from a Latin phrase in Isidore of Seville and turned into a person. His people are the Gaels, the last invasion and the ancestors of the historical Irish. He himself never comes; his uncle Ith sees Ireland from a tower in Spain, sails over, is killed by the Tuatha De out of jealousy, and Mil's eight sons come to avenge him. They win, and the Tuatha De go under the mounds. The whole scheme exists to connect the Irish to the Mediterranean and thence to Noah, which was what a respectable medieval origin story required, and it is one of the clearest cases in the pack of history written to order.
entities.variantTraditions: The derivation from Isidore is generally accepted. The supposed Spanish origin of the Irish has no basis in fact, though it has had a long afterlife in popular writing.

entities.name: Donn
entities.role: The first of the Milesians to die, who gathers the dead to his house in the sea
symbols: the rock Tech Duinn off the Kerry coast
entities.abode: Tech Duinn, the house of Donn
entities.bio: Drowned insulting the goddess of the land, and became the god the Irish dead go to.
entities.longBio: Donn is one of Mil's sons, and when the druidic storm hits the fleet he says something contemptuous about the Tuatha De and their arts, and is drowned for it. He is buried on a rock off the south-west coast, still called Tech Duinn, the house of Donn, and from his grave he says: to me, to my house, you shall all come after your deaths. That is very nearly the only statement in the whole Irish corpus of a plain god of the dead with a plain destination, and it survived in local belief into modern times, with the souls of the dead said to gather at that rock before departing. He is dark where the rest of the tradition is bright, and it is not clear whether he is old and mostly suppressed, or a late tidying-up.
entities.variantTraditions: Tech Duinn is identified with Bull Rock off the Beara peninsula. Whether Donn is an ancient god of the dead or a figure assembled by the Lebor Gabala compilers is disputed.

entities.name: The Cailleach
entities.role: The hag of winter, who made the landscape and lived seven lifetimes
entities.bio: She dropped stones from her apron to make mountains, ruled the winter half of the year, and grew young again each spring.
entities.longBio: The Cailleach belongs more to folklore than to the medieval manuscripts, and she is the more vital for it - she is attested from Kerry to the Hebrides and her name is written on the landscape in cairns, beds and chairs.
