She makes the country by accident, dropping stones from her apron as she strides, and she governs the winter, striking the ground with her hammer to harden it and washing her plaid in the whirlpool of Corryvreckan. In the Scottish versions she is transformed at Beltane into a young woman or turned to stone until winter returns, and she is set against Brigid, who holds the summer half. A famous ninth-century poem in her voice laments her lost youth with a directness almost nothing else in the corpus matches.
entities.variantTraditions: The Lament of the Old Woman of Beare is genuinely early and has a Christian frame - she has become a nun - which may or may not be original to it.

entities.name: Aine
entities.role: Goddess of summer, sovereignty and the sun, whose hill still keeps her name
epithets: queen of the fairies of Munster
entities.bio: A sovereignty goddess of Munster whose midsummer fires on her own hill were still being lit in the nineteenth century.
entities.longBio: Aine is associated with Cnoc Aine, a hill in County Limerick, where torches were carried around the hill at midsummer and afterwards through the fields and among the cattle - a practice recorded as still living in the 1870s. She is a goddess of the sun's warmth and of fertility rather than a solar deity in the Victorian sense. Several Munster families claimed descent from her, most famously the FitzGeralds, which is sovereignty theology surviving into Norman-Irish politics. One story has her raped by a king of Munster, whom she kills by biting off his ear - a king with a mutilated ear being disqualified from rule, which makes her revenge legally precise as well as personal.
entities.variantTraditions: Aine is sometimes given as a daughter of Manannan and sometimes conflated with Anu or Danu. The midsummer observances are well documented by nineteenth-century folklorists.

entities.name: Cliodhna
entities.role: Otherworld queen of south Munster, whose wave still bears her name
epithets: queen of the banshees of Munster
symbols: the three bright birds that heal with their singing
entities.abode: Tir Tairngire, and the rock at Glandore
entities.bio: She left the Otherworld for a mortal lover and was taken back by a wave that is still called after her.
entities.longBio: Cliodhna comes from Tir Tairngire, the land of promise, with a mortal man she has fallen in love with. He leaves her sleeping on the shore at Glandore in west Cork while he goes hunting, and a great wave comes in and carries her back, and that wave is called Tonn Chliodhna, one of the three great waves of Ireland, said to roar when a king of Munster is about to die. She keeps three brightly coloured birds that eat otherworldly apples and whose song heals the sick. In later folklore she becomes the queen of the fairies of south Munster and is the banshee of several families, and the Blarney Stone tradition attaches to her too. She is a good example of a figure whose cult is entirely local and entirely durable.
entities.variantTraditions: The Blarney Stone connection is late and probably invented for tourists, but her association with the wave at Glandore is old and consistent.

entities.name: Flidais
entities.role: Mistress of the wild things, whose cattle gave milk enough for an army
epithets: Flidais Foltchain, of the beautiful hair
symbols: the deer that draw her chariot
entities.bio: A goddess of woodland and deer in the old texts, and in the Ulster material a woman whose cattle-herd feeds an army.
entities.longBio: Flidais appears in the early glossaries as a goddess of wild things, with deer for her cattle and a chariot drawn by them, which has made her the standard Irish comparison for Artemis or Diana - though the resemblance is thinner than it looks. In the Ulster cycle she is a very different figure: a queen who elopes with Fergus mac Roich, bringing her herd with her, and whose cow Maol gives enough milk in one night to supply the whole of the Connacht army. The same text says that only she could satisfy Fergus, who otherwise required seven women. The two Flidais - woodland goddess and cattle-rich queen - may be one figure or may be two who share a name, and the sources give no help.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tain Bo Flidais survives in two very different recensions, and the goddess material and the saga material do not fit together comfortably.

entities.name: Crom Cruach
entities.role: The idol on the plain of Mag Slecht, said to take firstborn children
epithets: the bowed one of the mound
Cenn Cruaich, the head of the mound
domains: human sacrifice as the monks described it
symbols: the gold figure surrounded by twelve of stone
entities.bio: A gold idol with twelve stone figures around it, to whom the Irish are said to have sacrificed children for milk and corn - in texts written to condemn it.
entities.longBio: Crom Cruach stands on Mag Slecht, the plain of prostrations, a gold figure with twelve stone ones around it, and the Dindshenchas says the Irish gave a third of their healthy children to him for milk and corn, and broke their heads and shins bowing to him. Saint Patrick is said to have destroyed him with a sledgehammer. This entry comes with a large caution. The account is medieval Christian writing about the pagan past, in a genre with every motive to invent atrocities, and there is no archaeological evidence for systematic child sacrifice in Ireland. What the texts record is not what pre-Christian Irish people did, but what Christian Irish writers found it useful to say they had done - which is worth knowing as evidence of something else entirely.
entities.variantTraditions: The Crom Cruach material is late and polemical. Modern scholarship treats it as anti-pagan rhetoric rather than testimony, while noting that the site at Mag Slecht is real.

entities.name: Cu Chulainn
entities.role: The hound of Ulster: a boy who held an invasion at a ford, alone
symbols: the chariot and the two horses
entities.bio: Seventeen years old, exempt from the curse that flattened every other Ulsterman, he fought Medb's army one man at a time for months.
entities.longBio: Setanta kills the smith Culann's hound in self-defence and offers to guard the house himself until a replacement is reared, and takes the name Cu Chulainn from it. He is the son of Lugh by Deichtine, which puts a god behind him, and he trains in Scotland under the warrior-woman Scathach. When Macha's curse lays every Ulsterman on the ground in labour pains, he alone can stand, and he invokes single combat at a ford to hold Medb's whole army - one champion a day, for months, in winter. His battle-frenzy is the strangest thing in Irish literature: joints reverse, one eye sinks and the other protrudes, his hair stands with a drop of blood at each point, and a jet of dark blood rises from his skull. He dies tied upright to a standing stone so that he will not fall, and the enemy do not approach until a crow lands on his shoulder.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tain survives in three recensions differing considerably. Lady Gregory's version smooths the grotesque physical detail of the warp-spasm, which the earlier text dwells on.

entities.name: Conchobar mac Nessa
entities.role: King of Ulster, whose treatment of Deirdre destroyed his own court
domains: the ruin of his own house
symbols: the hall of the Red Branch
entities.bio: A capable king undone by insisting on a woman who did not want him, which cost him his best warriors.
entities.longBio: Conchobar gets the kingship by a trick of his mother Ness, who negotiates a single year of it for him and then makes it permanent. He rules Ulster from Emain Macha with the Red Branch warriors, and he is not a fool - the Tain shows him competent. But when Cathbad prophesies at Deirdre's birth that she will bring ruin, Conchobar's response is to keep her apart and raise her for himself, and when she elopes with Naoise he pursues them to Scotland, guarantees their safe return on the word of Fergus, and then has Naoise and his brothers killed anyway. Fergus and a third of the Ulster warriors go into exile with Medb over the broken guarantee, and it is those exiles who guide the invasion in the Tain. His breach of his own word is the wound the whole cycle bleeds from.
entities.variantTraditions: The manner of his death - a brain-ball lodged in his skull for years, bursting when he hears of the Crucifixion - is a Christian addition to an older story.

entities.name: Deirdre
entities.role: Deirdre of the Sorrows, who chose her own husband and was destroyed for it
symbols: the raven on snow with blood
entities.bio: Prophesied before birth to ruin Ulster, raised in seclusion for the king, she chose a younger man and it happened exactly as foretold.
entities.longBio: Cathbad prophesies at her birth that she will be beautiful beyond measure and that kings will war over her. The Ulstermen want her killed at once; Conchobar keeps her instead, raised apart, to be his wife when she is grown. She sees a raven drinking the blood of a calf on snow and says she would love a man with hair like the raven, cheek like the blood and body like the snow - and that is Naoise. She persuades him to take her, and they live in Scotland until Conchobar lures them back with a guarantee he breaks. Naoise is killed. Conchobar keeps her a year, in which she never smiles, and when he asks what she hates most and she says him and Eogan who killed Naoise, he gives her to Eogan for a year. She throws herself from the chariot and dashes her head on a rock.
entities.variantTraditions: In the earliest version she dies by her own hand on a stone; the later and more famous version has her die of grief on Naoise's grave, and Lady Gregory follows that one.

entities.name: Naoise
entities.role: Deirdre's husband, killed under a guarantee of safe conduct
entities.bio: He took Deirdre away because she gave him no choice, and came home on a promise that was not kept.
entities.longBio: Naoise is one of three sons of Usnech and a fine singer - the text says the cattle gave a third more milk for hearing him. Deirdre corners him and puts him under obligation by seizing his ears and threatening him with shame and mockery if he refuses her, which in this society is a real and binding pressure. They flee to Scotland with his brothers Ardan and Ainle, and live well until the king there wants Deirdre too, and they move on again. Conchobar sends Fergus with a guarantee of safe conduct. They come, Fergus is detained by a contrived obligation to attend an ale-feast, and the sons of Usnech are killed by Eogan mac Durthacht. Naoise is not a great warrior of the cycle and does not need to be; his function is to be a decent man caught between a woman's necessity and a king's word.
entities.variantTraditions: The Exile of the Sons of Usnech is one of the three sorrowful tales of Ireland, and the oldest version is terser and bleaker than the retellings.

entities.name: Fergus mac Roich
entities.role: The exiled king of Ulster who guided the invasion of his own country
symbols: the sword that made three strokes and cut hilltops off
entities.bio: He gave his word for Naoise's safety, Conchobar broke it, and he went over to Ulster's enemies and stayed there.
entities.longBio: Fergus was king of Ulster until Ness tricked him out of it for her son. He is enormous in every respect - the text says it takes seven women to satisfy him, that he eats seven pigs and drinks seven vats at a sitting, and his sword Caladbolg makes a stroke like a rainbow that takes the tops off three hills. When his guarantee to the sons of Usnech is broken he goes into exile with three thousand men and takes service with Medb, and it is Fergus who guides her army into Ulster during the Tain - and who repeatedly leads it astray to give Cu Chulainn time, because he fostered him. Medb takes him as a lover, and Ailill has his sword swapped for a wooden one before the great battle. When he faces Cu Chulainn, each yields to the other by prior agreement, and the war turns on it.
entities.variantTraditions: Caladbolg is generally accepted as related to the name Caledfwlch, which becomes Excalibur, though the weapons have nothing else in common.

entities.name: Medb
entities.role: Queen of Connacht, who started a war over a bull to stay equal with her husband
entities.bio: She counted her possessions against her husband's, found herself one bull short, and invaded Ulster to fix it.
entities.longBio: The Tain opens with pillow talk: Medb and Ailill compare what each brought to the marriage, and everything matches until the white-horned bull Finnbhennach, which had been in Medb's herds and left them because it would not be owned by a woman. Told there is an equal bull in Ulster, she assembles the armies of Ireland to take it. She is not a caricature - she leads from the front, negotiates, bribes, and reasons - but the text is clear that she will do anything, offering her daughter Finnabair to warrior after warrior as a fee for fighting Cu Chulainn, and offering herself. Her name means she who intoxicates and is related to mead, and behind the queen there is fairly clearly a sovereignty goddess: she is said to have slept with nine kings and that no man could rule Tara without her.
entities.variantTraditions: The reduction of a sovereignty goddess to a wilful queen is one of the standard moves of the Christian redactors, and Medb is the clearest example of it.

entities.name: Ailill mac Mata
entities.role: King of Connacht; Medb's husband, and steadier than he is given credit for
entities.bio: The husband in the pillow talk that started the war, who tolerated a great deal and eventually stopped tolerating it.
entities.longBio: Ailill is usually read as Medb's shadow, which underrates him. He is king of Connacht by marriage and knows it, and the Tain shows him managing a war he did not want with a wife he cannot control and an army full of Ulster exiles he cannot trust. He knows about Medb and Fergus and mostly says nothing; when he acts it is indirect, having Fergus's sword stolen and replaced with a wooden one before the decisive battle rather than confronting him. His own end is a long time coming: he is killed by Conall Cernach at Medb's instigation, or in revenge, depending on the version, and the sources disagree about who wanted it. He is the most recognisably ordinary person in a cycle full of monsters and demigods.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tain names more than one Ailill and the manuscripts confuse them; Ailill mac Mata of Connacht is the husband of Medb.

entities.name: Conall Cernach
entities.role: The champion of Ulster who avenged Cu Chulainn and collected heads
entities.bio: Cu Chulainn's foster-brother, sworn that whichever died first would be avenged by the other before the day was out.
entities.longBio: Conall is the second warrior of Ulster and would be the first anywhere else. He is bound to Cu Chulainn by a mutual oath of vengeance, and when Cu Chulainn is killed Conall hunts down every man involved, killing Lugaid mac Con Roi in a fight in which he gives up the use of one hand to make it fair because Lugaid has lost one. He returns to Emain Macha with the heads on a withe. In the Feast of Bricriu he is one of the three who compete for the champion's portion, and in Mac Datho's Pig he wins the right to carve by throwing the head of a man he killed that morning across the floor. He is a colder figure than Cu Chulainn and rather more frightening, because he is not driven by frenzy - he simply does what the obligation requires.
entities.variantTraditions: Conall appears in a great many stories of varying date, and his character is less consistent than Cu Chulainn's.

entities.name: Emer
entities.role: Cu Chulainn's wife, who out-argued him before she agreed to him
symbols: the knives of the fifty women
entities.bio: She courted in riddles, set him tasks that nearly killed him, and later gave up the man she had won rather than share him.
entities.longBio: Emer is chosen by Cu Chulainn because she is the only woman in Ireland who is his equal in the six gifts - beauty, voice, sweet speech, needlework, wisdom and chastity - and their courtship is conducted almost entirely in a coded language that the bystanders cannot follow. Her father, who does not want the match, sends Cu Chulainn to Scotland to train with Scathach in the hope that it kills him. It does not. Her finest moment is at the end of the Fand story: confronted with her husband's otherworldly lover, she comes with fifty women carrying knives, and then argues - that what is new is bright and what is familiar is honoured, and that she has been good to him and would be again. She wins, and Fand withdraws. She dies on Cu Chulainn's grave.
entities.variantTraditions: The Wooing of Emer survives in an early and a longer later version, the later one carrying most of the training-in-Scotland material.

entities.name: Scathach
entities.role: The warrior-woman of Skye who trained Cu Chulainn and gave him the Gae Bolg
entities.bio: The most formidable teacher in Irish literature: a woman who trained the greatest warriors of Ireland on an island in Scotland.
entities.longBio: To reach Scathach a student must cross the Bridge of Leaps, which throws off anyone who steps on it wrongly; Cu Chulainn manages it with the salmon-leap after several failures. She teaches him everything - the feats with named techniques, the thunder-feat, the apple-feat, the spear-cast from a chariot pole - and finally gives him the Gae Bolg, a spear thrown with the foot that opens into barbs inside the body and cannot be removed without cutting the man apart. She also prophesies his short and brilliant life. That the supreme martial authority of the tradition is a woman, and that this is treated as unremarkable, is one of the genuinely striking features of the Ulster material.
entities.variantTraditions: Her name means shadowy, and the connection to the Isle of Skye is traditional rather than textual; Dun Scaith on Skye is named for her but the association may be later.

entities.name: Aoife
entities.role: Scathach's rival, defeated by a trick, and mother of the son Cu Chulainn killed
epithets: the hardest woman warrior in the world
symbols: the chariot and horses she valued most
entities.bio: He beat her by asking, mid-fight, whether her chariot horses were falling - and threw her down while she looked.
entities.longBio: Aoife is Scathach's rival and, the text says, the hardest woman warrior in the world. When she and Scathach come to battle, Cu Chulainn fights her in single combat, and finding her his match he calls out that her chariot, horses and driver - the things she values most - have gone over a cliff. She glances, and he seizes her and carries her off. He spares her on terms, and she bears him a son, Connla. He leaves a ring and the instruction that the boy is to come to Ireland when it fits his finger, and is not to give way to any man, refuse a challenge, or tell his name. Those three conditions kill the child. Aoife's part is small and it sets the whole tragedy in motion.
entities.variantTraditions: Aoife of the Ulster cycle is a different figure from the Aoife who turns the children of Lir into swans, despite the shared name.

entities.name: Connla
entities.role: Cu Chulainn's son, killed by his father for refusing to give his name
entities.bio: Seven years old, bound by his father's own conditions not to name himself, he was killed by his father for keeping them.
entities.longBio: Connla comes to Ireland when the ring fits, under the three conditions Cu Chulainn laid down: never to give way, never to refuse a combat, never to tell his name. He lands and beats the champions sent to challenge him. Cu Chulainn goes down to the strand himself, and Emer begs him not to, because she has guessed. The boy will not name himself. They fight, and Connla is winning until Cu Chulainn uses the Gae Bolg, and only then, dying, does the boy say who he is. The whole thing is caused by the conditions the father set, which the son keeps perfectly. It is the Irish version of a story told from Persia to Germany, and this telling is the most economical: three rules, and each one is load-bearing.
entities.variantTraditions: The tale is Aided Oenfhir Aife, the death of Aoife's only son. Its relationship to the Persian Rostam and Sohrab story is a matter of shared type rather than demonstrated transmission.

entities.name: Ferdiad
entities.role: Cu Chulainn's foster-brother, forced to fight him at the ford for three days
symbols: the horn-skin no weapon could pierce
entities.bio: He refused the fight until Medb threatened him with the satire of poets, and then went, knowing how it would end.
entities.longBio: Ferdiad trained with Cu Chulainn under Scathach and they are foster-brothers, closer than kin. Medb needs someone who can hold him and works through everyone else first; when she comes to Ferdiad he refuses, and she offers Finnabair, and lands, and finally the thing that moves him - the threat that her poets will satirise him for cowardice, which would destroy his name and, in this world, his standing entirely. He goes. They fight three days at the ford, and each evening they stop, embrace, share food and send healing herbs across the water to each other. On the fourth day Cu Chulainn is losing and calls for the Gae Bolg. Afterwards he collapses over the body and speaks the lament that is the finest thing in the Tain - that it was all a game until Ferdiad came.
entities.variantTraditions: The Comrac Fir Diad is a late addition to the Tain, absent from the earliest recension, and is the most literary section of the whole work.

entities.name: Laeg
entities.role: Cu Chulainn's charioteer, who insulted him deliberately to keep him fighting
symbols: the grey of Macha and the black of Saingliu
entities.bio: The man who drove the chariot, watched everything, and knew exactly when to mock his master into standing up again.
entities.longBio: The charioteer in the Ulster cycle is not a servant but a professional and a confidant, and Laeg is the best of them. He drives the two great horses, he reports what he sees on the field in formal set-piece descriptions, and his particular skill is knowing when Cu Chulainn is flagging and needling him back into the fight - at the ford with Ferdiad he taunts his own master with cowardice, on purpose, and it works. He goes to the Otherworld ahead of Cu Chulainn in the Fand story and comes back with an account of it. He dies taking a spear meant for Cu Chulainn. The role tells you something about how these warriors actually functioned: nobody fought alone, and the man holding the reins was half the weapon.
entities.variantTraditions: The horses, the Grey of Macha and the Black of Saingliu, emerged from a lake and are treated as otherworldly; the Grey weeps blood before Cu Chulainn's death.

entities.name: Cathbad
entities.role: The druid whose prophecies were always right and never helped
epithets: father of Conchobar in some accounts
entities.bio: He told Deirdre's parents what she would cost them, and told a boy that whoever took arms that day would be famous and short-lived.
entities.longBio: Cathbad is the chief druid of Ulster and teaches a school of pupils. Two of his prophecies drive the cycle. The first is at Deirdre's birth, where he foretells the ruin she will bring and the Ulstermen want her killed. The second is casual: asked by a student what the day was good for, he says that a boy who takes up arms on it will have a name that outlasts everyone in Ireland and a short life. Cu Chulainn overhears, goes straight to Conchobar and asks for weapons. The pattern is exact - Cathbad speaks true, and the speaking is what makes it happen. He is also the one who curses the ground when Conchobar breaks his word over the sons of Usnech, and the curse takes, and Emain Macha never recovers.
entities.variantTraditions: Cathbad is named as Conchobar's father in some versions, making the king the son of a druid, which sits oddly with other accounts of Conchobar's conception.

entities.name: Bricriu
entities.role: Poison-tongue: he built a hall in order to start a fight in it
symbols: the champion's portion of the feast
entities.bio: He invited all Ulster to a feast and privately promised the champion's portion to three different men.
entities.longBio: Bricriu builds a magnificent hall with a balcony from which he can watch, invites the Ulstermen, and is told he may not stay because he cannot be trusted. He agrees to leave, and on his way out tells Loegaire, then Conall, then Cu Chulainn separately that the champion's portion is his. The resulting brawl runs the length of the story and is referred to three different judges, culminating in the beheading game: a stranger offers his head to anyone who will let him take theirs the next night. Only Cu Chulainn returns to keep the bargain, and is spared and named first champion. That episode reappears two and a half centuries later, almost move for move, as Sir Gawain and the Green Knight - one of the better-attested cases of Irish material reaching the French and English romances.
entities.variantTraditions: The transmission route from Fled Bricrenn to the Gawain poet is debated, but the structural identity of the beheading game is not.

entities.name: Cu Roi
entities.role: A king and sorcerer whose fortress turned all night, and who tested the champions
epithets: the churl in the grey mantle
symbols: the fortress that revolved at nightfall
the axe of the beheading game
entities.bio: He appeared as a giant churl with an axe to test which Ulsterman would keep a bargain that cost him his head.
entities.longBio: Cu Roi is a king of Munster and something considerably stranger - a sorcerer whose fortress spins every night so its entrance cannot be found, and who travels the world. He is the stranger who walks into Bricriu's hall as a monstrous churl and proposes the beheading bargain, and it is his judgement that settles the championship on Cu Chulainn. Later the two fall out over the division of spoils from a raid, including the woman Blathnat, and Cu Roi shaves Cu Chulainn's head and rubs cow dung into it, which is a considered insult rather than a killing. Blathnat, who wants to leave, betrays the secret of his life to Cu Chulainn - it is hidden in a salmon - and signals by pouring milk into the stream. He is killed, and his poet takes revenge by dragging her over a cliff with him.
entities.variantTraditions: The external soul hidden in an animal is a widespread folk motif; its appearance here is one of the earliest in Irish.

entities.name: The Brown Bull of Cuailnge
entities.role: The bull the whole war was fought for
symbols: the bellowing that carried across Ireland
entities.bio: An enormous bull that was once a man: he and his rival were swineherds who quarrelled through several lifetimes and shapes.
entities.longBio: Medb invades Ulster to take the Donn Cuailnge, and the text gives it a history that is stranger than the war. It and Finnbhennach were once two swineherds of rival lords, who quarrelled and fought each other through successive forms - as ravens, as sea creatures, as stags, as champions, as demons, as maggots - until each was swallowed by a cow and reborn as a bull. The Donn is carried off after Cu Chulainn falls, and when it meets Finnbhennach at Cruachan they fight the length of Ireland for a day and a night. The Donn wins, and scatters pieces of the white bull across the country, leaving place-names as it goes. Then it turns for home, and its heart bursts, and it dies. Nobody gains anything. That is the ending the Tain chooses.
entities.variantTraditions: The bull-quarrel prologue survives as a separate tale, and its relationship to the main narrative is one of the puzzles of the Tain's composition.

entities.name: The White-Horned Bull
entities.role: Medb's bull, who left her herd rather than be owned by a woman
domains: the cause of the pillow talk
entities.bio: The bull whose defection from Medb's herds to her husband's started a war.
entities.longBio: Finnbhennach was calved in Medb's herd and left it for Ailill's, because - the text says plainly - it would not remain the property of a woman. That single fact is what makes the inventory in the pillow talk come out uneven, and what makes Medb go after the Donn Cuailnge. Like its rival it was once a swineherd and has come through the same chain of transformations. At the end of the Tain the two bulls meet and fight across Ireland, and Finnbhennach is torn apart, its pieces dropped at places that are named for them afterwards. The war that killed thousands is settled by two animals in a night, and neither side gets a bull. The Tain is not a triumphalist text and its ending is one of the coldest in European literature.
entities.variantTraditions: The bull as the measure of a marriage's equality is not a metaphor the text explains, and the pillow-talk opening may be a later frame added to an existing raid narrative.

entities.name: Fionn mac Cumhaill
entities.role: Leader of the Fianna, who got his wisdom by burning his thumb on a fish
entities.bio: He cooked the salmon of knowledge for someone else, burned his thumb on it, and got the wisdom by accident.
entities.longBio: Fionn is raised in secret in the woods after his father's killing, and comes as a boy to the poet Finn Eces, who has spent seven years trying to catch the salmon of knowledge from the Boyne. The poet catches it and sets the boy to cook it, telling him not to eat any. Fat splashes on Fionn's thumb, he sucks it, and the knowledge is his; the poet, seeing it in his face, gives him the fish. Thereafter he can know anything by biting the thumb. He takes leadership of the Fianna, the warrior band that guards Ireland, by killing the fire-breathing Aillen who burns Tara every Samhain. The Fenian material is later, lighter and more popular than the Ulster cycle - closer to folklore than to saga, and it stayed alive in oral tradition in Ireland and Scotland into the twentieth century.
entities.variantTraditions: Fionn's name means fair or bright. The Ossianic poems James Macpherson published in the 1760s as ancient Gaelic epic were largely his own composition, and did enormous damage to the reputation of the genuine material.

entities.name: Oisin
entities.role: Fionn's son, the poet of the Fianna, who came back from the Otherworld three centuries late
symbols: the white horse that must not be dismounted
entities.bio: He spent what felt like three years in the land of the young, came home, touched the ground, and three hundred years fell on him at once.
entities.longBio: Oisin is Fionn's son by Sadhbh, born as a fawn and named the little deer. He is the poet of the Fianna and the one who survives it. Niamh of the Golden Hair takes him to Tir na nOg, where they live happily for what seems three years, and then he wants to see his father again. She gives him a white horse and one condition: he must not set foot on Irish soil. He finds the Fianna long gone and the country Christian, and stooping from the saddle to help some men lift a stone, his girth breaks. He touches the ground and becomes instantly ancient. In the Colloquy of the Ancients he then spends his last days in conversation with Saint Patrick, telling the old stories and arguing, sometimes bitterly, about whether the Fianna are in hell.
entities.variantTraditions: Acallam na Senorach, the Colloquy, is a large twelfth-century framing text; the debates with Patrick are the medieval Irish thinking about their own pagan past out loud.

entities.name: Oscar
entities.role: Fionn's grandson, the hardest fighter of the Fianna, killed at Gabhra
entities.bio: The strongest of the Fianna, who killed the High King at Gabhra and died of the wound he took doing it.
entities.longBio: Oscar is Oisin's son and the physical champion of the Fianna, described as the hardest fighter among them and reliably the one sent where the fighting is worst. His end comes at the battle of Gabhra, where the Fianna are broken by the High King Cairbre and the forces of the other warrior bands. Oscar and Cairbre kill each other. Fionn - in the versions where he is still alive - comes and weeps over him, and the text says that the only three times Fionn wept were for his hound Bran, for Oscar, and for one other. Gabhra is the end of the Fianna as an institution, and the Fenian cycle is unusual among Irish material in having a definite ending that everyone knows is coming.
entities.variantTraditions: The chronology of the Fenian cycle is inconsistent about whether Fionn is alive at Gabhra; different texts arrange it differently.

entities.name: Diarmuid Ua Duibhne
entities.role: The most loyal of the Fianna, who ran off with his chief's bride and died for it
symbols: the mark on his forehead no woman could see and not love
entities.bio: A magic mark made every woman love him, which is exactly the sort of gift that ends badly.
entities.longBio: Diarmuid has a love spot on his forehead - got from an otherworldly girl - and any woman who sees it loves him helplessly. At the feast where the ageing Fionn is to be betrothed to the young Grainne, she sees it, drugs the whole hall, and puts Diarmuid under geis to take her away. He refuses, because Fionn is his chief; the geis leaves him no choice. They are pursued across Ireland for sixteen years, sleeping in a different place every night, and the dolmens all over Ireland are still called the beds of Diarmuid and Grainne. Peace is eventually made. Then Fionn takes him hunting a boar he is forbidden by geis to hunt, and Diarmuid is gored. Fionn can heal any man with water carried in his hands, and twice he lets the water run through his fingers, and Diarmuid dies.
entities.variantTraditions: Toraigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghrainne is late, sixteenth-century in its surviving form, but the pursuit motif is much older and clearly related to the Deirdre story.

entities.name: Grainne
entities.role: Betrothed to an old man, she put a younger one under obligation and ran
entities.bio: She drugged an entire wedding feast and used a binding obligation to force the man she wanted to take her.
entities.longBio: Grainne is Cormac mac Airt's daughter, promised to Fionn, who is old enough to be her grandfather. At the betrothal feast she asks who each of the Fianna is, sees Diarmuid's love spot, and acts: she drugs everyone in the hall except a handful, and puts Diarmuid under geis - a binding she can impose and he cannot refuse without disgrace - to take her out of it. He goes, unwilling. The pursuit lasts sixteen years. The most quoted moment comes when a splash of water reaches her thigh as they cross a stream, and she remarks that the water is bolder than Diarmuid has been - which is the point at which their relationship changes. After his death she is eventually reconciled with Fionn and marries him, and the Fianna laugh at her for it. She is one of the few women in the corpus who is entirely the author of her own story.
entities.variantTraditions: Grainne's name is sometimes connected with grain and with a sun goddess; the connection is speculative and rests mainly on etymology.

entities.name: Caoilte mac Ronain
entities.role: The fastest of the Fianna, who survived to tell Saint Patrick everything
domains: the telling of the old stories
symbols: the road covered faster than a horse
entities.bio: He could outrun anything, and outlived his entire generation to become the memory of it.
entities.longBio: Caoilte is Fionn's nephew and the fastest man in Ireland - sent for anything that must be fetched quickly, and in one story he gathers a pair of every wild animal in the country in a single day to pay a ransom. His importance is at the end rather than the middle. In the Colloquy of the Ancients he and Oisin, impossibly old, travel Ireland with Saint Patrick, and at each place Caoilte tells the story of what happened there and how it got its name. Patrick's guardian angels tell him it is right to write it all down. The whole enormous text is a device for preserving pagan tradition with clerical permission, and Caoilte is its main voice - the survivor whose job is to remember accurately.
entities.variantTraditions: The Acallam is one of the largest surviving Irish texts and its frame is doing visible ideological work, licensing the material it preserves.

entities.name: Sadhbh
entities.role: Turned into a deer by a druid she refused, and mother of Oisin
symbols: the doe that would not be hunted
entities.abode: The Hill of Allen, then the woods
entities.bio: She came to Fionn as a deer his hounds would not touch, and was taken back to the woods when he was away.
entities.longBio: Sadhbh refuses the Dark Druid and is turned into a deer for it. Fionn's hounds Bran and Sceolan, who were themselves born human, corner her and will not harm her, and she comes into his house and becomes a woman again while she is inside it. They are happy, and she is pregnant, and then Fionn goes away to fight. The druid takes the shape of Fionn and calls her out, and the moment she crosses the threshold she is a deer again and is driven off. Fionn searches for seven years and finds nothing. Then his hounds corner a naked boy in the woods who has been raised by a doe, and that is Oisin. Sadhbh is never found. It is one of the few stories in the cycle with no resolution at all.
entities.variantTraditions: Sadhbh's name means goodness or sweetness. The story survives chiefly in later and folk versions rather than early manuscript.

entities.name: Niamh
entities.role: Niamh of the Golden Hair, who took Oisin to the land of the young
symbols: the white horse that crosses the sea
entities.bio: She rode out of the sea on a white horse, chose Oisin, and warned him about the one thing that would undo it.
entities.longBio: Niamh comes on a white horse across the waves and asks for Oisin by name, offering him Tir na nOg, the land of the young, where nobody ages or sickens. He goes. They are happy for what he takes to be three years. When he wants to see Ireland again she does not forbid it - she gives him the horse and one instruction, that he must not let his foot touch Irish ground, and tells him plainly what will happen if he does. He does, and it does. Niamh is not a temptress or a trap; she is honest with him throughout, and the tragedy is entirely a matter of time running at different rates in the two countries. The motif is old and international, and this is one of its cleanest tellings.
entities.variantTraditions: The Oisin in Tir na nOg poem is eighteenth-century in its familiar form, by Micheal Coimin, though the underlying story is much older.

entities.name: Goll mac Morna
entities.role: The one-eyed rival who killed Fionn's father and then served him for years
entities.bio: He killed Fionn's father and led the Fianna until Fionn came of age, and then served under him, mostly.
entities.longBio: Goll's name means one-eyed and he was called Aed until he lost the eye. He kills Cumhall, Fionn's father, at the battle of Cnucha and takes leadership of the Fianna, and when Fionn grows up and claims his place, Goll steps aside and follows him - which is not the obvious move and the texts do not fully explain it. The truce is real but never comfortable, and the rivalry between clan Baiscne and clan Morna runs under the whole cycle, surfacing periodically in quarrels over spoils and precedence. In one late tradition it breaks out finally and Goll is besieged on a rock and starves rather than surrender. He is the most interesting secondary figure in the Fenian material precisely because he is not a villain.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between Goll and Fionn is handled differently across texts, from open enmity to genuine loyalty.

entities.name: Aillen
entities.role: The burner: he lulled Tara to sleep with music every Samhain and set it alight
symbols: the harp that puts everyone to sleep
entities.bio: Killing him is how Fionn got command of the Fianna: he stayed awake by pressing a spear-point to his own forehead.
entities.longBio: Every Samhain for twenty-three years Aillen comes out of the sidhe, plays music that puts everyone at Tara to sleep, and burns the place down. Fionn offers to deal with him in exchange for his father's position. He is given a spear whose point is so venomous that pressing his forehead against it keeps him awake through the music - the pain defeats the enchantment. When Aillen sees his fire will not take he flees for the mound, and Fionn kills him at the entrance with the spear and brings the head to Tara. It is a compact and satisfying piece of storytelling: the enchantment is beaten not by counter-magic but by a man deliberately hurting himself, which is very much the Fenian way of solving things.
entities.variantTraditions: The spear is Birgha, given by Fiacha; in some versions the wakefulness comes from a cloak or a different object entirely.

entities.name: Bran and Sceolan
entities.role: Fionn's two hounds, who were born human
entities.bio: His aunt was turned into a hound while pregnant, and her pups were born as dogs and stayed that way.
entities.longBio: Tuiren, Fionn's aunt, is turned into a hound by a jealous woman of the sidhe while pregnant, and gives birth in that shape. She is restored; the pups are not, and Fionn keeps them. Bran and Sceolan are therefore his first cousins, and the fact explains why they will not harm Sadhbh when she comes as a deer, and why they find Oisin in the woods - they know their own kin whatever shape it is in. Bran is the greater of the two, described with a yellow body, red ears and green feet, the standard Irish colouring for an otherworldly animal. Fionn's grief when Bran dies is one of the three times he is said to have wept. The Fenian cycle takes dogs seriously in a way the other cycles do not.
entities.variantTraditions: The story of Tuiren survives in late versions; the hounds themselves are constant across the whole Fenian tradition.

entities.name: Cormac mac Airt
entities.role: The ideal High King, who got a golden cup that broke apart at a lie
symbols: the cup that shatters at falsehood
the silver branch with three apples
entities.bio: The model of a just king, whose test of truth was a cup that fell to pieces when three lies were told over it.
entities.longBio: Cormac is the High King the tradition holds up as the standard - the reign under which the land was fertile because the king was just, which is sovereignty theology working as designed. Manannan comes to him with a silver branch of three golden apples whose music takes away sorrow, and trades it for three wishes, then takes his wife, son and daughter. Following them, Cormac reaches Manannan's house and is shown a series of images he cannot interpret, and is given a golden cup that breaks into three when three lies are spoken over it and mends when three truths are. His family is returned. His own end is domestic and strange: he chokes on a salmon bone, and having converted to a belief in one God before Patrick's arrival, he asks not to be buried at the pagan cemetery, and the river rises three times to prevent it.
entities.variantTraditions: The Teagasc an Riogh, a wisdom text of instructions attributed to Cormac, is genuinely early and is one of the best sources for what the Irish thought a king was for.

entities.name: Conaire Mor
entities.role: The perfect king destroyed by having to break his own prohibitions one by one
domains: the inevitability of the broken taboo
entities.bio: Every prohibition laid on him is broken in a single evening, most of them by his trying to be merciful.
entities.longBio: Conaire's father was a bird-man, and at his making he is given a list of geasa: never to go right-hand-wise round Tara and left-hand-wise round Bregia, never to hunt the beasts of Cerna, never to let three red men go before him into a red man's house, and several more. His reign is famously good. Then his foster-brothers take to raiding, and rather than execute them he exiles them - and the mercy is what begins it. Forced by circumstances he cannot control, he breaks each geis in turn on a single day, and ends at Da Derga's hostel, besieged, with three red men having ridden in before him. He dies of thirst in the middle of the fight because every river in Ireland hides itself from the man carrying his cup. It is the most tightly constructed tragedy in Irish literature.
entities.variantTraditions: Togail Bruidne Da Derga is early and its language is difficult; the accumulation of geasa is deliberate and the text is precise about which is broken when.

entities.name: Niall of the Nine Hostages
entities.role: He kissed a hag at a well and she became the sovereignty of Ireland
epithets: the ancestor of the Ui Neill
symbols: the hag who becomes a beautiful woman
entities.bio: Four brothers refused the hideous woman guarding the well; he did not, and she turned into sovereignty itself.
entities.longBio: Niall and his four half-brothers, out hunting, are thirsty, and find a well guarded by a woman described in the ugliest terms the text can manage - black, bristled, green-toothed. She will give water only for a kiss. Three refuse outright; one gives her a token peck. Niall kisses her properly and lies with her, and she becomes the most beautiful woman in the world and tells him she is Sovereignty, and that as she was first ugly and then lovely, so kingship is won by hard fighting before it becomes fair. His descendants, the Ui Neill, dominated Ireland for six centuries, which is the point of the story - it is a dynastic charter. The same motif appears in English as the Wife of Bath's Tale and the ballad of the Loathly Lady.
entities.variantTraditions: Niall is probably historical, a fourth or fifth-century king; the well story is a legitimation legend attached to him later.

entities.name: Suibhne
entities.role: A king cursed into madness who lived in the treetops and made poetry there
symbols: the leaping from tree to tree
entities.bio: He threw a cleric's psalter into a lake and killed his servant, and was cursed to live as a bird-man in the woods.
entities.longBio: Suibhne, king of Dal nAraidi, attacks Saint Ronan for founding a church on his land, throws his psalter into a lake and kills one of his people. Ronan curses him to wander naked and mad, and in the battle of Mag Rath the curse takes: he rises into the air and lives thereafter in the treetops, feathered, leaping from yew to yew, unable to bear the company of people. What makes Buile Shuibhne remarkable is that the madness produces poetry - long passages of the finest nature verse in early Irish, in his voice, praising the trees and the cold water and the stags, interspersed with his misery. He is eventually reconciled and killed by a swineherd's spear. It is a text about exile and about the value of what exile makes, and it is why Flann O'Brien and Seamus Heaney both went back to it.
entities.variantTraditions: Buile Shuibhne is a twelfth-century text about a seventh-century battle. Heaney's Sweeney Astray is the best-known modern rendering.

entities.name: Bran mac Febail
entities.role: He sailed west to the islands and came home to find he could not land
symbols: the silver branch with white blossom
entities.bio: A woman with a silver branch sang him a description of the islands, and he sailed, and could never come back properly.
entities.longBio: A woman appears in Bran's hall with a branch of silver and white blossom and sings fifty quatrains about the islands in the west - the plain of delight, the island of joy, the land where there is no sorrow. He sails with twenty-seven companions. On the way he meets Manannan driving a chariot over the sea, who tells him that what Bran sees as water is a flowering plain to him. They reach the Island of Women and stay what feels like a year. When one man's homesickness takes them back to Ireland, people on the shore say they know of Bran mac Febail only from ancient stories; a man who leaps ashore turns to ashes at once. Bran writes the account in ogham, tells it from the boat, and sails away, and nobody knows where.
entities.variantTraditions: The Immram Brain is early, seventh or eighth century, and the Christian stanzas about Christ inserted into Manannan's speech are widely thought to be a later addition.

entities.name: Don
entities.role: Mother of the Welsh divine family, as shadowy as her Irish counterpart
epithets: mother of the children of Don
entities.bio: The ancestress the Welsh gods are named for, who does nothing in any surviving story.
entities.longBio: Don occupies exactly the position in Welsh material that Danu occupies in Irish: her children - Gwydion, Arianrhod, Gilfaethwy, Gofannon, Amaethon - are the divine family of the Fourth Branch, and she herself never appears. The parallel with Danu is close enough that scholars have long treated them as the same figure under two names, and the parallel between Gofannon and Goibniu the smith supports it. But it is a parallel of position and etymology, not of story, and it should not be pushed. Whether the Welsh material preserves gods at all is disputed: the Four Branches were written down in the eleventh or twelfth century as literature, and their characters may be remembered deities, or may be characters.
entities.variantTraditions: The equation of Don with Danu is standard in older scholarship and treated more cautiously now. Neither has a narrative.

entities.name: Math fab Mathonwy
entities.role: Lord of Gwynedd, who had to keep his feet in a virgin's lap except in war
entities.bio: A king under a strange condition, whose nephews engineered a war so he would have to stand up.
entities.longBio: Math cannot live unless his feet lie in the lap of a virgin, except when war prevents it. His nephew Gilfaethwy desires the footholder Goewin, and Gwydion contrives a war with the south by stealing Pryderi's pigs, so that Math must go and fight; in his absence Gilfaethwy rapes Goewin. Math's response is the strangest punishment in Welsh literature: he turns the two brothers into a pair of deer, then boar, then wolves, one male and one female each time, requiring them to mate and bear young, swapping sexes each year for three years. Then he restores them. He also marries Goewin to make good what was done to her in his own household. He is a magician of the first rank and his judgements are exact, which makes him the moral centre of the Fourth Branch.
entities.variantTraditions: The footholding condition is unexplained in the text and has no parallel elsewhere; suggestions that it is a garbled ritual are guesses.

entities.name: Gwydion
entities.role: Magician, thief and storyteller, who arranged everything in the Fourth Branch
epithets: the best teller of tales in the world
symbols: the twelve horses and hounds made from mushrooms
entities.bio: He conjured an army's worth of horses out of fungus to buy stolen pigs, and started a war doing it.
entities.longBio: Gwydion is the engine of the Fourth Branch. He hears of pigs sent from Annwn to Pryderi, goes south disguised as a bard - and is described as the best teller of tales in the world - and conjures twelve horses and twelve hounds with gilded trappings out of mushrooms to trade for them, warning that his creation will not last a day. It doesn't; war follows; Pryderi is killed. All of it was arranged to get Math out of the way for his brother. Punished, restored, he then becomes the maker of his sister's son: he tricks Arianrhod into naming Lleu and arming him, and with Math conjures a wife for him out of flowers. He is not a moral figure and the text does not pretend he is, but he is the most inventive character in Welsh literature.
entities.variantTraditions: The old reading of Gwydion as a Welsh Odin or a culture-hero is Victorian. The Milky Way is called Caer Gwydion in Welsh.

entities.name: Arianrhod
entities.role: She refused her son a name, arms and a wife, and was outmanoeuvred on all three
entities.bio: Humiliated by a test she was made to take, she laid three impossible conditions on the child of it.
entities.longBio: Math needs a new footholder and Gwydion proposes Arianrhod. Math asks whether she is a virgin, she says she believes so, and he tells her to step over his bent wand. She does, and drops a boy child who is baptised as Dylan and makes for the sea, and a small second thing that Gwydion snatches up and hides in a chest. That is Lleu. Arianrhod's response to the whole humiliation is to swear three destinies on the child: that he shall have no name unless she gives it, no arms unless she arms him, and no wife of any race on this earth. Gwydion defeats each by trickery. Reading her as a villain is easy and probably wrong - she was subjected to a virginity test in front of a court and then handed the resulting child's future, and the three prohibitions are the only power she has.
entities.variantTraditions: Caer Arianrhod is a real reef off the Caernarfonshire coast, visible at low tide. Her name means silver wheel and has attracted a great deal of speculative lunar interpretation.

entities.name: Lleu Llaw Gyffes
entities.role: The bright one of the skilful hand, who could only be killed in an impossible way
epithets: the fair one with the skilful hand
symbols: the spear made only on Sundays during mass
entities.bio: The terms of his death were so absurd that describing them to his wife was what got him killed.
entities.longBio: Named, armed and married by Gwydion's trickery against his mother's prohibitions, Lleu is given a wife made of flowers. She wants someone else, and asks how he could be killed, and he explains at length: not indoors nor out, not on horseback nor on foot, only by a spear a year in the making and worked only during Sunday mass, and only if he stands with one foot on a bath's edge and one on a goat's back under a thatched roof by a river. She has all of it prepared and asks him to demonstrate. Speared, he becomes an eagle and flies off; Gwydion tracks him by a sow eating the maggots dropping from him, and finds him rotting in an oak, and sings him down. He is restored and kills the man who did it. The name is cognate with Lugh's but the stories are unrelated.
entities.variantTraditions: The Lleu-Lugh equation is linguistically contested; Lleu and Llew, lion, are confused in the manuscripts, which produced the persistent mistranslation Llew Llaw Gyffes.

entities.name: Blodeuwedd
entities.role: A woman conjured out of flowers, who was not consulted about any of it
entities.bio: Made from oak, broom and meadowsweet to be a wife, she chose someone else and was turned into an owl for it.
entities.longBio: Because Arianrhod has sworn that Lleu shall have no wife of any race on this earth, Math and Gwydion take the flowers of the oak, the broom and the meadowsweet and make a woman from them. Nobody asks her anything. She meets Gronw Pebr while Lleu is away, and they agree to be rid of him, and she extracts the elaborate conditions of his death and arranges every one. When Lleu is restored, Gwydion catches her and tells her he will not kill her - he will do something worse - and turns her into an owl, never to show her face in daylight, shunned by all other birds. Her name shifts from flower-face to owl in the same word. Modern readers tend to find her the most sympathetic figure in the Fourth Branch and the medieval text plainly does not intend that, which is worth noticing rather than smoothing over.
entities.variantTraditions: Blodeuwedd was central to Robert Graves's White Goddess, which is a work of poetic imagination rather than scholarship and should not be used as a source on her.

entities.name: Pwyll
entities.role: Prince of Dyfed, who swapped bodies with the lord of the underworld for a year
entities.bio: He wronged Arawn by accident, made it right by taking his place for a year, and slept beside Arawn's wife without touching her.
entities.longBio: Pwyll drives another man's hounds off a stag, and the man is Arawn, king of Annwn. To make amends he agrees to exchange shapes and kingdoms for a year and to kill Arawn's enemy at the end of it. What makes the story is that he shares a bed with Arawn's wife every night for that year and turns his face to the wall each time, saying nothing to her - and when the year is up Arawn learns of it and their friendship is permanent. Afterwards Pwyll sits on the mound at Arberth, where anyone who sits either receives blows or sees a wonder, and sees Rhiannon riding past at a pace no horse can catch until he thinks to ask her to stop. He then nearly loses her by promising a boon to a stranger without hearing it first, which the text treats as characteristic.
entities.variantTraditions: The First Branch is the most morally coherent of the four, and the year in Annwn is one of the few genuinely amiable episodes in the Mabinogi.

entities.name: Rhiannon
entities.role: The lady on the white horse, punished for a crime that never happened
symbols: the white horse that cannot be overtaken
the three birds whose song wakes the dead
entities.bio: Her infant son vanished, her women framed her, and she spent years carrying visitors to the gate on her back.
entities.longBio: Rhiannon rides past the mound at Arberth on a white horse at a walking pace that no rider can catch, and cannot be overtaken until Pwyll simply asks her to stop - which tells you what kind of story this is. She chooses him over the man she was betrothed to. Their son disappears on the night he is born, and the six women set to watch smear puppy blood on the sleeping mother's face and swear she destroyed him. Her penance is to sit at the mounting block by the gate, tell every visitor the story, and offer to carry them to the court on her back. She does it for years without complaint. The boy is found and returned by Teyrnon, who had rescued him from a monstrous claw at the foaling of a mare - the child and the colt taken the same night, which is the horse connection stated as plainly as the text ever does.
entities.variantTraditions: Rhiannon is generally connected to the Gaulish horse goddess Epona and to a reconstructed Rigantona, great queen; the etymology is good and the identification is inference.

entities.name: Pryderi
entities.role: The only character in all four Branches, and he dies badly in the last one
entities.bio: Stolen at birth, raised by strangers, restored, and killed years later in a magical duel over stolen pigs.
entities.longBio: Pryderi is taken on the night of his birth and found by Teyrnon in a stable, wrapped in silk, at the moment a monstrous claw reaches in for a newborn colt. He is raised as Gwri Golden-hair, grows at an unnatural rate, and is returned when Teyrnon sees his resemblance to Pwyll. He rules Dyfed after his father. In the Third Branch he and Manawydan find the country emptied of people by an enchantment, and Pryderi is trapped by a golden bowl that fixes his hands to it and his feet to the floor, and vanishes. In the Fourth he is killed by Gwydion in single combat, by magic rather than strength, over the pigs Gwydion stole from him. He is the thread that runs through all four Branches, which is why they are thought to have once been a single narrative.
entities.variantTraditions: That Pryderi appears in all four Branches is the main evidence for reading them as a unified composition rather than four separate tales.

entities.name: Bran the Blessed
entities.role: A giant king of Britain whose severed head talked pleasantly for eighty-seven years
symbols: the cauldron that revives the dead without speech
the bridge he made of himself
entities.bio: Too big for any house, he lay across a river as a bridge for his army - and after death his head kept them company for decades.
entities.longBio: Bran is a giant, king of the Island of the Mighty, and no house has ever been built that could hold him. He gives his sister Branwen to the king of Ireland, and gives him too the cauldron that brings dead men back to life without the power of speech. When Branwen is mistreated he takes an army across, wading the sea, lying down across the Shannon so his men can cross on him - saying that he who would be a leader must be a bridge. The war ruins both islands. Wounded by a poisoned spear, he tells his seven survivors to cut off his head and carry it, and it goes on talking, as good company as ever, for seven years at Harlech and eighty at Gwales, until someone opens the forbidden door. Then they bury it facing France, and it wards Britain until Arthur digs it up out of pride.
entities.variantTraditions: The talking head and the buried head warding the island are among the oldest-looking elements in the Mabinogi. The Bran-Bron-Grail connection proposed by some scholars is speculative.

entities.name: Branwen
entities.role: Married to Ireland, beaten daily in the kitchen, she trained a starling to carry a message
epithets: one of the three chief ladies of the island
entities.bio: Three years of humiliation, and she got word home by teaching a bird to talk and telling it where to fly.
entities.longBio: Branwen is married to Matholwch of Ireland to bind the two islands, and the alliance is poisoned at once when her half-brother Efnysien, insulted at not being consulted, mutilates the Irish horses. Compensation is paid but the shame is not forgotten, and in Ireland she is put out of the king's chamber, set to work in the kitchen, and struck by the butcher every day. She rears a starling at the edge of her kneading trough, teaches it to speak, describes her brother to it, and sends it across with a letter under its wing. Bran comes with an army. The war destroys nearly everyone - five pregnant women survive in Ireland, seven men in Britain. Branwen comes home, looks at both islands, says that two good islands have been laid waste because of her, and her heart breaks. She is buried in a four-sided grave on the Alaw.
entities.variantTraditions: A Bronze Age urn was excavated at a site on Anglesey traditionally called Branwen's grave in 1813, which proves the tradition is old rather than that the story is true.

entities.name: Manawydan
entities.role: Bran's brother, who defeated an enchantment by threatening to hang a mouse
epithets: one of the three ungrasping chieftains
entities.bio: With his country emptied by magic and his family gone, he took up shoemaking, and then out-lawyered a wizard over a mouse.
entities.longBio: Manawydan survives the Irish war, marries Rhiannon, and settles in Dyfed - and then a mist falls and every person and animal in the country vanishes. He and Pryderi try trades in England and are driven out of each town for being too good at them. Pryderi and Rhiannon are taken by the enchantment. Left alone, Manawydan sows three fields of wheat, and mice strip two of them; he catches one slow pregnant mouse and sets up a tiny gallows on the mound at Arberth to hang it as a thief. Three churchmen appear in succession offering to buy its life, and he refuses each until the last, a bishop, admits he is the enchanter Llwyd, that the mouse is his wife, and that the whole desolation was revenge for Rhiannon's old betrothed. Manawydan names his terms precisely, and everything is restored. He wins by procedure.
entities.variantTraditions: Manawydan shares Manannan's name and father and has essentially no other resemblance to him: no sea, no magic, no Otherworld. The Third Branch is the least supernatural of the four.

entities.name: Efnysien
entities.role: The half-brother who wrecked two kingdoms and destroyed the cauldron to make it right
symbols: the cauldron he broke by getting into it
entities.bio: He started the war by mutilating horses over a slight, and ended it by letting himself be thrown into the cauldron.
entities.longBio: Efnysien is not consulted about his sister's marriage, and his response is to cut the lips, ears, eyelids and tails off the Irish horses in the stable - a piece of gratuitous cruelty that poisons the alliance permanently. Later, in the hall in Ireland, he crushes a man's head in his hands, and throws Branwen's young son Gwern into the fire, which begins the general slaughter. Then, seeing the Irish dead being fed into the cauldron of rebirth and coming out to fight again, he hides among the corpses, is thrown in, and stretches himself until the cauldron bursts into four pieces and his own heart breaks. He is the most purely destructive figure in Welsh literature and his last act is the one that gives his side a chance. The text does not explain him and does not try.
entities.variantTraditions: Efnysien and his brother Nysien are presented as opposites, one who makes peace and one who makes trouble; only Efnysien is developed.

entities.name: Arawn
entities.role: King of Annwn, who lent his kingdom and his face to a man who had wronged him
symbols: the white hounds with red ears
entities.bio: The lord of the Welsh otherworld, whose hounds are white with red ears and whose response to insult was an exchange of places.
entities.longBio: Arawn's hounds are white with red ears, the standard Welsh marker of an otherworldly animal, and Pwyll's driving them off their kill is the insult that starts the First Branch. His remedy is elegant: they exchange shapes and kingdoms for a year, Pwyll must kill Arawn's rival Hafgan with a single blow and refuse to strike a second, and at the end they resume their own lives. Annwn in this telling is not a hell or a land of the dead but another kingdom, with a court and a queen and hunting and politics, adjacent rather than below. Arawn behaves impeccably throughout and the friendship holds afterwards. In later Welsh tradition the ruler of Annwn becomes Gwyn ap Nudd instead, and Arawn recedes.
entities.variantTraditions: Annwn is sometimes conflated with the Christian hell in later Welsh writing, which the Mabinogi itself does not do.

entities.name: Gwyn ap Nudd
entities.role: Lord of Annwn and the wild hunt, condemned to fight the same duel every May Day forever
entities.bio: He and his rival must fight for the same woman every first of May until the end of the world.
entities.longBio: Gwyn takes over from Arawn as ruler of Annwn in later Welsh tradition, and becomes the leader of the wild hunt, riding with the Cwn Annwn, the hounds of the otherworld, whose cry is heard before a death. In Culhwch and Olwen he abducts Creiddylad, and Arthur's judgement is that he and Gwythyr must fight for her every May Day until Judgement Day, and whoever wins on that last day shall have her - a permanent, formalised, entirely unresolvable seasonal combat. His court is placed under Glastonbury Tor, and a story of Saint Collen visiting it and dispersing the illusion with holy water is one of the sharper encounters between the two religions in Welsh writing. He is also said to gather the souls of the dead and, in one line, to be set over the brood of devils to keep them from destroying the world.
entities.variantTraditions: Nudd is cognate with the Irish Nuada and the British Nodens; Gwyn's own name means white or bright.

entities.name: Ceridwen
entities.role: She brewed a year's inspiration for her ugly son and a servant boy got all of it
symbols: the cauldron stirred for a year and a day
entities.bio: Three drops of a year-long brew landed on the wrong thumb, and she chased the boy through four shapes to eat him.
entities.longBio: Ceridwen's son Morfran is so ugly that she sets about brewing a potion to give him all knowledge instead, which must be stirred for a year and a day and yields only three drops. She sets the boy Gwion Bach to stir. At the end three drops spit onto his thumb, he sucks it, and the knowledge is his - and the rest of the cauldron turns to poison. She chases him: he becomes a hare, she a greyhound; a fish, she an otter; a bird, she a hawk; a grain of wheat, and she a hen, and eats him. Nine months later she bears him and cannot bring herself to kill the child, so she puts him in a leather bag in the sea, and he is found and becomes Taliesin. The shape-chase is one of the oldest motifs in the tradition and this is its best-known version.
entities.variantTraditions: The Tale of Taliesin survives only in late manuscripts, sixteenth century onward, and Ceridwen's promotion to a major goddess in modern paganism has no medieval basis.

entities.name: Taliesin
entities.role: The radiant brow: a real sixth-century poet who became a magical one
entities.abode: The court of Maelgwn, and Elffin's weir
entities.bio: Found in a bag at a salmon weir by a man who had caught nothing, and he began composing at once.
entities.longBio: There was a real Taliesin, a sixth-century court poet of the northern British kingdoms, and some poems in the Book of Taliesin are plausibly his. The legendary Taliesin is another matter: he is Gwion Bach reborn from Ceridwen, cast into the sea, and found by Elffin at a salmon weir on May eve, and he consoles his finder with a poem from inside the bag. At Maelgwn's court he silences twenty-four bards by playing a note that makes them all say blerwm, and frees his patron with verse. The poems in his voice claim every existence - that he was at the crucifixion, at the tower of Nimrod, in the ark, that he has been an eagle, a stag, a word in a book. That register, the poet claiming all times and shapes at once, is closely related to Amergin's song and is one of the striking survivals of the tradition.
entities.variantTraditions: The historical and legendary Taliesins are quite separate. The Book of Taliesin is a fourteenth-century manuscript containing material of very mixed date.
